votes.discussion_detail: Adopted Comprehensive Plan Community Goals and Objectives including Audubon Society biodiversity revisions.

votes.item_title: Item 41: Alternative Motion — Excuse Annexation and Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with Bertha Gamble (Durham Code Sec. 70-129(9))
votes.discussion_detail: Excused annexation requirement based on revenue-negative fiscal impact analysis and authorized City Manager to enter into a water utility extension agreement for 1518 Hamlin Road.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: 1051 Olive Branch Road Environmental Protections, Grave Relocation, and Suburban Housing Supply (Item 43)
disagreements.summary: Council held a prolonged debate over Pulte Home Company LLC's 284-unit annexation at 1051 Olive Branch Road, pitting housing-supply concerns against East Durham Open Space Plan incompatibility, mass grading, peripheral tree save, and relocation of an on-site cemetery, resulting in continuance to September 7.
disagreements.side_a_position: Continue the hearing to seek stronger tree preservation, environmental mitigation, and cemetery/community commitments without immediately killing needed housing stock.
side_a_arguments: Javiera Caballero (02:49:21) and Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson (03:08:56) stressed Durham's worsening housing shortage while agreeing existing open questions justified a continuance.

Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:13:19) argued $230k-$300k housing expands supply for working-class firefighters, teachers, and officers while still expressing concern over the gravesite and the negligible 21%-to-22% tree-save increase.

Mayor Steve Schewel (03:04:54) backed increasing supply in Southeast Durham but warned he would vote no immediately given the 'not compatible with East Durham Open Space Plan' staff finding and environmental sensitivity.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose or demand deep substantive redesigns addressing far-flung Southeast Durham sprawl, cost-burden spillover, climate/mass-grading harm, and cemetery removal.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece (02:57:53) questioned whether townhouses in far-east Durham near Morrisville actually curb gentrification in Braggtown or Walltown and argued annexation conferred no net benefit to Durham.

DeDreana Freeman (02:23:07, 03:10:27) highlighted cumulative impacts across nine area rezonings, carbon footprint without transit, nearby cost-burdened neighborhoods, and distress over moving a historic cemetery—noting she only supported a continuance if meaningful tree-save and stream-crossing changes returned.
disagreements.resolution: With applicant Tim Sivers' agreement (03:23:52), Council left the public hearing open and continued Item 43 to September 7, 2021.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Duke School $10M Tax-Exempt Revenue Bond Host-Approval Resolution (Item 45)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to pass the federal TEFRA resolution for private Duke School's revenue bonds, with Javiera Caballero voting Nay and Mark-Anthony Middleton raising equity concerns about private tuition and public-service reliance.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the routine ministerial TEFRA resolution because the City of Durham incurs zero debt, financial obligation, or taxpayer liability.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (03:41:30), Pierce Freelon (03:39:47), DeDreana Freeman (03:42:27), and Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:42:00) agreed that federal tax-law pass-through approval carries no city financial risk, though Middleton pressed Duke School officials on $20k-$23k tuition, lack of free/reduced lunch or busing, and reliance on city police/fire.
disagreements.side_b_position: Decline to lend City host-jurisdiction TEFRA approval to a private school revenue bond issuance.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero cast the sole Nay vote on roll call (03:43:18) without stating floor remarks.
disagreements.resolution: TEFRA resolution passed 6-1.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Premise and Efficacy of Municipal Corporate Incentives (Item 46 CARsgen Therapeutics)
disagreements.summary: While Council approved the $256,000 CARsgen Therapeutics incentive, members clashed philosophically over the 'but-for' constitutional fiction behind local corporate cash incentives versus net tax-revenue math.
disagreements.side_a_position: Vote Aye only under deep protest because municipal bidding wars force Durham into logically flawed cash giveaways to multi-billion-dollar firms.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (03:55:54, 04:00:19) argued a newly Hong Kong-listed company valued over $2B clearly did not need $256,000 from Durham 'but for' the grant to locate here, urging federal/state reform while voting yes to avoid losing jobs to competing states.
Jillian Johnson (03:57:50) concurred with Reece's protest.
disagreements.side_b_position: Support economic development incentives as pragmatic capital-leveraging investments yielding positive net property-tax returns and local jobs.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:58:10, 04:01:57) rejected characterizing incentives as morally questionable, noted finance projections showed tax revenues exceeding the $256,000 payout within three years, and urged coupling incentives with vocational training for Durham residents without college degrees (echoing Donald Hughes).
disagreements.resolution: Council approved the $256,000 incentive agreement.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Longtime Homeowner Grant Program Expansion: Citywide vs. Targeted Equity and Staff Capacity
disagreements.summary: Following Charlie Reece's proposal to hold applications open and rapidly craft a temporary citywide homeowner tax-relief program ahead of the joint City-County program, Council debated equity targeting, included neighborhoods (Braggtown, Merrick-Moore, Walltown), and Community Development staffing capacity.
disagreements.side_a_position: Create a temporary citywide property-tax relief program for the 2020-21 gap year to ensure all burdened longtime low-income homeowners qualify legally and equitably until the joint County program improves.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (04:11:36, 04:18:09, 04:32:16) argued citywide investments city-wide justify legal defensibility whereas ad-hoc neighborhood additions face legal hurdles cited by Assistant City Attorney Krista Kucera, offering to sunset the city program once the County raises AMI limits and benefit caps.
DeDreana Freeman (04:16:52, 04:27:11, 04:50:24) prioritized immediate gap-year relief so Braggtown, Merrick-Moore, and Walltown residents are not left out of 2019-2020 tax cycles.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep the 2019 cycle under current parameters through August 31 and avoid a rushed citywide expansion without staff capacity, cost modeling, and equity targeting.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (04:23:20, 04:41:41, 04:51:47) argued against blanket 'equality' floodgates in affluent areas in favor of targeted 'equity' investments (sidewalks, safety, targeted relief) in historically disinvested neighborhoods, citing Reginald Johnson's staffing constraints.

Jillian Johnson (04:28:51, 04:35:56), Pierce Freelon (04:45:52), and Steve Schewel (04:37:30, 04:48:50) respected staff capacity warnings (vacancies from retirement and medical leave) and supported letting the current program finish through Aug. 31 while directing staff to return in early August with a scoping and resource plan-to-make-a-plan.
disagreements.resolution: Council reached consensus thumbs-up (04:53:00-04:53:17) allowing staff to extend current applications administratively to August 31 and bring an assessment/scoping timeline for gap-year options to the first August work session.

meetings.title: Special Virtual Durham City Council & the Durham Board of County Commissioners Meeting June 15, 2021
meetings.executive_summary: BOCC Chair Brenda Howerton and Durham Mayor Steve Schewel co-presided over the June 15, 2021 joint virtual public hearing of the Durham City Council and Board of County Commissioners on the Comprehensive Plan's revised Community Goals and Objectives, with all seven Council members participating. Planning staffer Kayla Seibel presented two years of outreach involving roughly 850 residents and Engagement Ambassadors, plus post-Planning Commission edits addressing equity, resident voice, history, and growth management following the Planning Commission's 10-1 endorsement. During the public hearing, residents raised concerns regarding biodiversity/bird-friendly protections, growth management, equity, and public safety, prompting staff to present specific biodiversity and native-plant text additions. No formal votes were taken—as separate votes were scheduled for Council on June 21 and BOCC on June 28—but Mayor Schewel confirmed unanimous Council thumbs-up support for incorporating staff's biodiversity edits into the adoption packet.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Joint Roll Call (City Council and BOCC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: BOCC Chair Brenda Howerton called the historic joint virtual session to order alongside Mayor Steve Schewel, with quorum confirmed for both boards and Council Member Pierce Freelon joining at 00:02:18. Clerks acknowledged all participating City Council members, BOCC commissioners, City Manager Wanda Page, and Interim County Manager Claudia Hager.

agenda_items.title: Staff Presentation: Comprehensive Plan Revised Community Goals and Objectives
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning team member Kayla Seibel detailed public engagement dating back to summer 2019—including roughly 850 residents across engagement ambassador sessions and eight focus groups—achieving at least 77% agreement across draft objectives. Staff highlighted revisions addressing land-use/transportation coordination, non-displacement, growth management, sustainability, and edits added after the Planning Commission's April 27 public hearing (where the Commission recommended approval 10-1).

agenda_items.title: Joint Public Hearing and Elected Official Feedback on Biodiversity and Process Integrity
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Residents spoke on biodiversity, native ecosystems, equitable development, and policy implementation, including New Hope Audubon / Bird-Friendly Durham input and specific wording requests from speaker Mr. Kopec. Staff presented additive biodiversity, native-plant, public-space, and school edits while advising against last-minute deletions that would strip community-vetted language; Mayor Schewel obtained thumbs-up consensus from City Council to include the staff-drafted biodiversity attachment ahead of the June 21 adoption vote.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No formal vote (informal Council thumbs-up on biodiversity edits)

meetings.title: FY22 Budget Council Follow-Up Meeting June 10, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the June 10, 2021 FY22 Budget Council Follow-Up Meeting with all seven council members participating to finalize unresolved items ahead of the June 21 budget vote. Council agreed by consensus to defer the Master Aging Plan request to a future work session and voted 7-0 on the meeting's sole formal roll-call motion—moved by Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and seconded by Mark-Anthony Middleton—to adopt Option 4 for ARPA-funded employee premium pay ($5.9 million) and Option C to double pay-for-performance bonuses ($6.3 million across funds). Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson and 911 Director Randy Beeman briefed Council on emergency call center staffing and cellular misrouting, while Interim County Manager Claudia Hager, Tax Administrator Dwayne Brinson, and DSS Director Ben Rose presented a $1.25 million joint City-County Longtime Homeowner Tax Grant pilot ($750k County / $500k City, 30% AMI, $750 cap), which Council urged the County to expand toward 60% AMI and a higher cap. Council also debated but deferred votes on Pierce Freelon's proposal to make Council seats full-time with staggered pay increases, and heard sharp exchanges between Middleton and departing Police Chief C.J. Davis regarding gun violence, ShotSpotter, and 911 calls.

agenda_items.title: Opening Remarks and Consensus Deferral of Master Aging Plan Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the follow-up session aiming to resolve all remaining FY22 budget questions prior to the June 21 vote. With Council thumbs-up consensus, Council agreed to defer the late-arriving Master Aging Plan funding request until advocates can present at a future work session with staff analysis.

agenda_items.title: HR Presentation and Vote: FY22 Employee Premium Pay (Option 4) and Pay-for-Performance Bonuses (Option C)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR Director Regina Youngblood presented four ARPA-funded premium pay options (covering 1,361 full-time and 59 part-time eligible employees) and three fund-balance pay-for-performance bonus options alongside the 2% general / 4% police-fire base pay plan. While noting next year's budget must restore full base-pay step progress, Council voted unanimously 7-0 to adopt Option 4 for premium pay ($5.9 million total) and Option C doubling performance bonuses ($6.3 million total; $4.6 million General Fund).

agenda_items.title: 911 Emergency Communications Center Staffing and Operations Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson and 911 Director Randy Beeman addressed concerns about 911 wait times, explaining that Durham's center answers 100% of incoming calls, has no voicemail, relies on ESInet routing, and experienced isolated cases where cell towers routed callers to neighboring jurisdictions. Beeman also outlined the 12-week academy and floor-shadowing pipeline for new call-takers.

agenda_items.title: Joint City-County Longtime Homeowner Tax Grant Pilot (County Presentation) and City Program Options
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim County Manager Claudia Hager, County Tax Administrator Dwayne Brinson, and DSS Director Ben Rose presented a Mecklenburg-inspired, DSS-administered property tax grant pilot ($750k County + $500k City, targeting homeowners ≤30% AMI with 10+ years residency, capped at $750/year) to replace the underutilized 2020 deferral program. Council praised the County's pivot while unanimously pressing BOCC to raise income eligibility to 60%–80% AMI and increase the $750 grant cap, and debated whether to maintain a parallel citywide expansion with payment sent directly to the tax office.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (resolution to BOCC drafted)

agenda_items.title: Discussion of Proposal to Increase City Council Member Salaries
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Pierce Freelon advocated raising City Council pay to full-time levels—backed by Javiera Caballero's suggestion of phasing in raises by staggered 2023/2025 cycles so voters judge incumbents first—arguing low pay creates an equity barrier for working-class candidates. DeDreana Freeman prioritized staff base pay over council raises, while Middleton and Johnson raised legal/incumbency-optics questions and the lack of a full-board vote readiness, deferring the item to a future work session.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (deferred to work session)

agenda_items.title: Gun Violence, ShotSpotter Rollout, Police Chief C.J. Davis Update, and 'We Are the Ones'
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton urged urgent summer gun-violence action—calling on residents to dial 911 when hearing gunfire regardless of disagreements over ShotSpotter—and questioned departing Police Chief C.J. Davis on whether ShotSpotter alerts elicit different officer responses than human 911 calls. Council Member Pierce Freelon also requested a work-session follow-up on fully funding the 'We Are the Ones' violence-prevention request before adjournment.

votes.item_title: Approve FY22 Budget Inclusion of Option 4 for Premium Pay ($5.9M ARPA) and Option C for Pay-for-Performance Bonuses ($6.3M)
votes.notes: Unanimous 7-0 roll call vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted the highest staff-presented compensation bonus tiers (Option 4 ARPA-funded premium pay plus Option C doubled pay-for-performance bonuses) while committing to prioritize recurring base-pay plan restoration in FY23.

disagreements.meeting_title: FY22 Budget Council Follow-Up Meeting June 10, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Proposal to Increase City Council Member Salaries to Full-Time Pay
disagreements.summary: Council members disagreed over the urgency, timing, and optics of raising City Council compensation to full-time levels ahead of the FY22 budget adoption.
disagreements.side_a_position: Advance a full-time Council salary structure—potentially phased in across staggered 2023/2025 election cycles—so lower-income and working-class residents are not priced out of serving.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon argued Council pay is an equity barrier preventing eligible working residents from running and wanted to set the wheels in motion sooner rather than waiting until 2027.
Javiera Caballero proposed a staggered approach (2023 for at-large seats, 2025/2027) and noted comparable cities like Wilmington/New Hanover and Charlotte pay significantly more.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer or oppose immediate Council raises, prioritizing city staff base pay and ensuring any Council raise only takes effect after all sitting members face voters.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman stated she would much rather direct scarce recurring dollars to city staff base pay than to Council salaries.

Mark-Anthony Middleton cited incumbency advantage and preferred any raise take effect no earlier than 2023 after a full election cycle; Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and staff noted legal uncertainty over staggered pay and that two members had stepped away during the vote readiness check.
disagreements.resolution: No vote was taken; the proposal was referred to a future work session pending legal guidance from the City Attorney's Office.

disagreements.meeting_title: FY22 Budget Council Follow-Up Meeting June 10, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Citywide Expansion vs. County-Led Implementation of Longtime Homeowner Tax Relief
disagreements.summary: While all members wanted stronger property tax relief for longtime low-income homeowners, Council weighed whether to keep running a separate citywide program immediately or rely on the County's $1.25M DSS-administered grant while pressing BOCC to raise the 30% AMI ceiling.
disagreements.side_a_position: Partner through the County's DSS-administered tax grant program (sending a formal resolution urging BOCC to raise eligibility to 60% AMI) rather than rushing an unvetted standalone citywide expansion.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel and Charlie Reece noted state constitutional limits require a clear public-purpose legal nexus (making DSS welfare administration safer than direct city checks) and urged focusing immediate advocacy on raising the County pilot from 30% to 60% AMI.
Jillian Johnson suggested reviewing the current city pilot's results after summer break while keeping pressure on the County to scale up.
disagreements.side_b_position: Move proactively on citywide or neighborhood-expanded tax relief and ensure residents experiencing hardship have immediate local access without restrictive caps.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman argued gentrification affects residents across Durham and expressed concern about delaying relief or limiting caps below $1,000–$1,400.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Mayor Pro Tem Johnson agreed to coordinate with Mayor Schewel on transmitting a resolution to BOCC urging a 60% AMI threshold ahead of the County's June 14 budget vote.

meetings.title: Virtual City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the June 10, 2021 Virtual City Council Work Session, Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson called the meeting to order before Mayor Steve Schewel assumed the chair, and Council reviewed upcoming resolutions on HB 324 and the federal American Jobs Plan, suspended the rules to affirm two board/commission appointments (Shanika Bynum and Donald A. Hughes), and accepted the City Manager's priority agenda items covering ARPA grant ordinances, the FY 2021-22 budget and CIP, affordable housing loans (Commerce Street Apartments, Commerce Street Seniors, Elizabeth Street Apartments), $263 million in water and sewer revenue refunding bonds, Comprehensive Plan goals, and an economic development incentive agreement with Karsten Therapeutics Limited. After a lengthy budget deliberation on funding community/youth programming ('We Are The Ones' / ongoing mini-grant program), Council passed a compromise motion 6-1 to allocate an additional $187,600 from one-time city fund balance (bringing total funding to $250,000) specifically restricted to mini-grants. On that 6-1 split vote, Pierce Freelon moved the measure, DeDreana Freeman seconded it, and Mark-Anthony Middleton voiced support for the $250,000 funding level, while Steve Schewel had earlier advocated a $100,000 direct appropriation and concerns were raised about earmarking funds before contract review; the individual roll-call breakdown of the 6 Ayes versus 1 Nay was omitted in a transcript digest gap. Council concluded by unanimously settling (7-0) the June 21, 2021 City Council meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements: HB 324 Resolution & American Jobs Plan Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman reported that Durham Public Schools Board member Jovonia Lewis had taken the lead on drafting an HB 324 resolution, which Freeman planned to circulate to Council soon. Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson introduced a resolution supporting the Biden administration's $2 trillion American Jobs Plan, highlighting home care workers with Fight for 15, and asked the Clerk to add it to the upcoming Monday night City Council agenda by consensus.

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Appointments (Shanika Bynum and Donald A. Hughes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel and Council Member Pierce Freelon addressed two appointments (Shanika Bynum and Donald A. Hughes) that needed to be affirmed during the work session. Council voted by roll call to suspend the rules and then voted by roll call to affirm both appointments.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (Roll Call; tally omitted in transcript gap)

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items & June 21 Agenda Preview (ARPA, Budget/CIP, Housing Loans, $263M Bonds, Comprehensive Plan, Karsten Therapeutics)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager presented priority updates for upcoming agenda items, including Recovery and Renewal Task Force (RRTF) requests for the Convention Center Complex and Rediscover Durham, affordable housing loan commitments (Commerce Street Apartments for DHA, Commerce Street Seniors, and Elizabeth Street Apartments LLC), a resolution for up to $263 million in Water and Sewer Utility System Revenue Refunding Bonds (Series 2021), Comprehensive Plan community goals and objectives, and an incentive agreement with Karsten Therapeutics Limited. Council unanimously accepted the priority items (7-0) and reviewed consent/departmental items including Item 8 (ARPA 2021 grant ordinance and FY 2021-22 budget/CIP) and Item 24 (Durham City Transit Company insurance letter of credit), pulling Item 12 (Commerce Street Apartments) for discussion.

agenda_items.title: FY 2021-22 Budget Allocation: 'We Are The Ones' / Grassroots Mini-Grant Funding
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle portion of the work session, Council and staff debated whether to place $250,000 in unauthorized budget reserve pending nonprofit contract review or directly appropriate funds for immediate summer youth and community work. Mayor Steve Schewel proposed appropriating $100,000 into the ongoing mini-grant program (in addition to an existing $60,000), while Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton argued the problem required the full $250,000 level. Council Member Pierce Freelon moved to add $187,600 (rounding to $250,000 total) strictly for mini-grants, which passed 6-1 with staff clarifying the funds would come from one-time city fund balance rather than ARPA.

agenda_items.title: Settle Agenda for June 21, 2021 City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager presented the finalized agenda for the June 21, 2021 City Council meeting, consisting of Consent Agenda items 1 through 38 and General Business Agenda public hearings items 40 through 46. Council voted unanimously to settle the agenda, confirmed no budget loose ends remained with staff, and adjourned at 4:59 PM.

votes.discussion_detail: Council accepted the City Manager's priority items covering RRTF requests, DHA Commerce Street Apartments, Commerce Street Seniors, Elizabeth Street Apartments, $263M water/sewer refunding bonds, Comprehensive Plan presentation, and Karsten Therapeutics Limited.

votes.item_title: FY 2021-22 Budget Addition of $187,600 for 'We Are The Ones' / Mini-Grants (Total $250,000)
votes.notes: Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson presided over this vote and announced 'the motion passes 6 to 1' at 03:55:26. Individual member names on the roll call were truncated by a [gap omitted] marker between 03:55:01 and 03:55:21, leaving only the final unattributed response ('I will not.') visible, so individual ayes/nays arrays are left empty rather than inferred.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual City Council Work Session
disagreements.issue: FY 2021-22 Budget Allocation for 'We Are The Ones' / Grassroots Mini-Grants
disagreements.summary: Council members differed on the funding amount and mechanism for a community/youth engagement proposal ('We Are The Ones') and ongoing mini-grant program. Some expressed discomfort earmarking $250,000 for the full program without further scope and contract review, and Mayor Steve Schewel proposed appropriating $100,000 directly into existing mini-grants instead, while Council Members Mark-Anthony Middleton and Pierce Freelon pushed for the full $250,000 level. Freelon's compromise motion adding $187,600 restricted solely to mini-grants passed 6-1.
disagreements.side_a_position: Appropriate $187,600 additional funding (to reach $250,000 total) in the FY 2021-22 budget restricted to grassroots mini-grants
side_a_arguments: Community needs and summer youth work are urgent and justify the full $250,000 funding level
Black women and grassroots community organizers should not have to struggle for modest funding compared to other city expenditures
Restricting the $187,600 addition strictly to mini-grants addresses colleagues' concerns about unreviewed components of the broader proposal while allowing immediate planning
disagreements.side_b_position: Limit immediate appropriation to $100,000 or withhold earmarking for unreviewed program components pending scope and contracting review
side_b_arguments: Discomfort earmarking $250,000 for a specific nonprofit program without further review of scope of work and contract terms
Alternative proposal to directly appropriate $100,000 into the already-ongoing mini-grant program rather than placing $250,000 in unauthorized reserve
disagreements.resolution: Pierce Freelon's compromise motion to add $187,600 (bringing total funding to $250,000) from one-time city fund balance strictly for mini-grants passed 6-1 at 03:55:26; individual roll-call names were omitted in a transcript digest gap.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council June 10, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the June 10, 2021 City Council Work Session—where Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson called the meeting to order before Mayor Steve Schewel presided and later traded the gavel back to Johnson during Council salary and violence-prevention items—Council passed four unanimous 7-0 procedural roll-call votes (suspending rules for Citizens Advisory Committee corrections, appointing Shena M. Bham and Donald A. Hughes, accepting City Manager priority items, and setting the June 21 regular meeting docket). By unanimous 7-0 thumbs-up consensus, Council also directed the City Manager to remove the Main Street 'Defund' pavement painting within a month after June 25 and commission a post-George Floyd protest mural, scheduled resolutions backing the American Jobs Plan and opposing NC HB 324, and agreed to park roughly $80,000 in 'appropriations not authorized' pending public engagement and a November vote on Council living-wage pay. Following intense debate over timing, public input, ARPA eligibility, and program scope, Council voted 6-1 (Mayor Steve Schewel dissenting) to allocate an additional $187,600 from one-time fund balance—bringing FY22 funding to $250,000—strictly for 'We Are The Ones' violence-prevention mini-grants.

agenda_items.title: Priority Resolutions, CAC Rule Suspension & Appointments, and Manager Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson called the session to order at 1:01 PM before Mayor Steve Schewel assumed the chair (Pierce Freelon arrived at 00:09:28). Council added an American Jobs Plan resolution by consensus, voted 7-0 to suspend rules and appoint Shena M. Bham and Donald A. Hughes to the Citizens Advisory Committee, and voted 7-0 to accept City Manager Priority Items.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 7-0 across three procedural Roll Call votes

agenda_items.title: Fayetteville Street Corridor Safety, 911 Shortages, and Durham YouthWorks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Gwendolyn Bookman requested dedicated foot and bike patrols along the Fayetteville Street corridor, Erica Schurz raised alarm over 911 call-center staffing shortages, and Donald Hughes advocated expanding the Durham YouthWorks summer jobs program.

agenda_items.title: Commerce St & Elizabeth St Housing Loans (12, 17), Morreene Rd Sewer Loan (19), Trails (30), and 160D Codes (31-32)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled and reviewed several June 21 Consent items, including DHA's Commerce Street Apartments (Item 12), Elizabeth Street Apartments (Item 17), a $2.3 million loan to DHA for Morreene Road Apartments sanitary sewer replacement (Item 19), Third Fork Creek Phase 2 Trail engineering (Item 30), and Chapter 160D housing/unsafe-building code amendments (Items 31-32).

agenda_items.title: Durham Police Department Community Services Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Incoming Interim Police Chief Shari Montgomery and DPD staff presented on Durham Police Department community services, youth outreach, and neighborhood engagement programs.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Community Goals and Objectives Preview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Carl Kolosna and Lisa Miller previewed the draft Comprehensive Plan Community Goals and Objectives ahead of the joint June 15 public hearing and June 21 Council vote.

agenda_items.title: Main Street 'Defund' Pavement Painting Removal & Mural Consensus, and HB 324 Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: By a unanimous 7-0 thumbs-up consensus, Council directed the administration to remove the worn Main Street 'Defund' pavement painting within one month after June 25 and commission a permanent mural honoring post-George Floyd protests. Council also agreed to add a supplemental resolution opposing NC House Bill 324 (02:39:23).

agenda_items.title: City Council Living-Wage Compensation Timing and Public Engagement Reserve
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson chairing, Pierce Freelon and Javiera Caballero urged moving toward a ~$35,000 living-wage Council salary in 2022 rather than waiting until 2024 so candidates without independent wealth are not priced out, while Charlie Reece, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Steve Schewel opposed unvetted mid-budget self-raises. Council reached consensus to reserve roughly $80,000 in 'appropriations not authorized' pending public engagement and a November 2021 post-election vote.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Consensus to reserve ~$80,000 for November 2021 vote

agenda_items.title: Additional $187,600 Allocation from Fund Balance for 'We Are The Ones' Violence Prevention Mini-Grants
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated expanding FY22 violence-prevention funding beyond the $62,400 already budgeted for the 'We Are The Ones' initiative after ARPA eligibility questions arose with Budget Director Bertha Johnson. Narrowing the motion strictly to mini-grants rather than mutual-aid or community centers, Council voted 6-1 to allocate an additional $187,600 from one-time fund balance to reach $250,000 total, with Mayor Steve Schewel dissenting.

agenda_items.title: Approval of June 21 Regular City Council Meeting Docket and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel resumed the chair, received the board nominations report, and presided over a 7-0 roll-call vote settling the June 21 regular meeting agenda (Consent Items 1-38 and GBA Hearings 40-46) before adjourning at 4:59 PM.

votes.discussion_detail: Suspended rules during the work session to consider corrected Citizens Advisory Committee nominations immediately.

votes.item_title: Appoint Shena M. Bham and Donald A. Hughes to the Citizens Advisory Committee
votes.discussion_detail: Confirmed appointments of Shena M. Bham and Donald A. Hughes to the Citizens Advisory Committee following rule suspension.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager Priority Items
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted priority additions submitted by the City Manager for the June 21 docket.

votes.item_title: Allocate Additional $187,600 from One-Time Fund Balance to 'We Are The Ones' Violence Prevention Mini-Grants ($250,000 Total)
votes.notes: Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson presided during this vote (03:54:09-03:55:03).
votes.discussion_detail: Directed an extra $187,600 (spoken approximately as '$187.8k rounding out to $250,000' above $62,400 already budgeted) from one-time fund balance exclusively for mini-grants under the 'We Are The Ones' program, excluding mutual aid and community center components.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 10, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Timing, Tiering, and Public Input for City Council Living-Wage Compensation Increases
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether to raise Council salaries to a ~$35,000 living wage starting in 2022 or defer any raise until after public engagement and the 2021 election.
disagreements.side_a_position: Move forward promptly toward a ~$35,000 living-wage base in 2022 so working-class candidates and sitting members without independent wealth can afford to serve.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon and Javiera Caballero argued that low part-time stipends exclude lower-income residents from running or remaining on Council and urged an earlier 2022 effective date rather than waiting until 2024.
disagreements.side_b_position: Do not enact unvetted mid-budget raises or tiered salaries before the municipal election; defer to public input and a post-election November vote.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece, Steve Schewel, and Mark-Anthony Middleton opposed voting themselves a mid-budget raise without prior public budget engagement, and Middleton also objected to tiered salary levels.
disagreements.resolution: By consensus (03:10:40-03:14:51), Council set aside roughly $80,000 in 'appropriations not authorized' in the FY22 budget to preserve funding capacity for a November 2021 vote after public engagement.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 10, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: 'We Are The Ones' Violence Prevention Funding Amount, Fund Source, and Scope (Mini-Grants vs. Mutual Aid/Centers)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 6-1 over how much extra money to allocate from fund balance—versus ARPA—and whether funding should be restricted strictly to mini-grants.
disagreements.side_a_position: Provide an extra $187,600 from fund balance to bring 'We Are The Ones' mini-grants to $250,000 total immediately in FY22.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon, DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Charlie Reece, and Mark-Anthony Middleton supported reaching $250,000 immediately to empower grassroots violence-prevention mini-grants rather than deferring to uncertain ARPA scoring.

Restricting the $250,000 allocation to mini-grants addressed concerns from Budget Director Bertha Johnson and Javiera Caballero regarding ARPA procurement and unvetted mutual-aid or center line items.
disagreements.side_b_position: Limit extra one-time fund-balance dollars to $100,000 rather than $187,600 and scrutinize program design before committing $250,000.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel favored adding $100,000 rather than $187,600 to reach $250,000 and cast the sole Nay vote when the $187,600 mini-grant motion was called.
disagreements.resolution: Council passed the $187,600 mini-grant allocation 6-1, with Steve Schewel dissenting.

meetings.title: Budget Healing Event June 8, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: On June 8, 2021, the City of Durham launched Part 1 of its Budget Healing Series focused on participatory community guidance for more than $51 million in City American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds (alongside more than $61 million for Durham County), hosted and opened by Council Member Pierce Freelon. Following an opening song ('Lift Every Voice and Sing' led by Nnenna Freelon), Pierce Freelon delivered a land acknowledgment and historical reflection on Hayti and urban renewal before announcing a quarterly Budget Healing cadence. NCCU professors Dr. Jim Harper II and Dr. Henry McKoy presented historical and racial economic-equity data, and Interim Deputy City Manager Bertha Johnson outlined ARPA categories and the fall allocation timeline, before SpiritHouse co-director Nia Wilson led a healing meditation ahead of community breakout sessions.

agenda_items.title: Musical Opening, Land Acknowledgment, Urban Renewal Context, and Quarterly Series Launch
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Pierce Freelon welcomed residents to the first Budget Healing Event after Nnenna Freelon performed 'Lift Every Voice and Sing.' Freelon offered a land acknowledgment, spoke on the historical destruction of Hayti during urban renewal, and announced quarterly community budget healing sessions to democratize ARPA planning.

agenda_items.title: NCCU Presentations on Hayti History, Poverty Disparities, and Economic Inclusion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: FUSE fellow Leela Pedersen introduced NCCU history chair Dr. Jim Harper II and entrepreneurship director Dr. Henry McKoy. Dr. Harper reviewed Juneteenth and Black Wall Street history prior to urban renewal, while Dr. McKoy presented racial poverty and equity-index data showing stark disparities between White and Black/Hispanic households in Durham and urged community-led economic ecosystems.

agenda_items.title: Budget Office Briefing on Durham's ARPA Allocation, Timeline, and Equity Contacts
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Deputy City Manager Bertha Johnson explained federal ARPA eligible uses and an allocation exceeding $51 million for the City (and $61 million for the County), alongside the April-September 2021 vetting and voting schedule. Johnson also recognized City and County equity leads Sharon Williams and Kweli Rashied-Henry and shared the online portal for resident proposals.

agenda_items.title: SpiritHouse Healing Meditation and Facilitated Community Breakout Dialogues
agenda_items.discussion_summary: SpiritHouse co-director Nia Wilson guided attendees through a grounding reflection confronting redlining and cultural suppression before participants moved into facilitated breakout dialogues on local budget priorities.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council June 7, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the June 7, 2021 virtual City Council meeting with six members present after voting 6-0 to excuse Charlie Reece's absence. Following proclamations honoring outgoing Planning Commissioner Tom Miller ('Tom Miller Day'), National Gun Violence Awareness Day, and Juneteenth 2021, Council unanimously approved the consent agenda (6-0) and Item 30 (6-0, approving a Durham Central Park easement and development agreement with Lambert Development Hunt Street II LLC that increased its Affordable Housing Fund contribution from $57,000 to $285,000). Under Item 39, Council held the final public hearing on the proposed FY21-22 budget and FY22-27 CIP—hearing roughly 40 speakers largely divided over reallocating 60 vacant police positions to unarmed crisis responders and ShotSpotter—before approving Item 40 (Cabarrus/Caviness Avenue tier boundary change) 6-0. On Item 41 (Rollingdale II rezoning for 33 townhomes at 602–606 W. NC-54 Hwy), Council passed both the UDO/FLUM rezoning and consistency statement by 5-1 split votes—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Pierce Freelon, and Mark-Anthony Middleton voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting Nay—before unanimously approving HUD CARES Act Second Substantial Amendment motions (6-0 each) and entering closed session (6-0).

agenda_items.title: Excused Absence for Charlie Reece and Proclamations (Tom Miller Day, Gun Violence Awareness Day, Juneteenth 2021)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 6-0 to excuse Charlie Reece for his absence (noting parliamentary clarification that future late arrivals should simply be recorded in minutes). Mayor Steve Schewel issued proclamations honoring retiring Planning Commissioner Tom Miller, proclaiming June 4, 2021 as National Gun Violence Awareness Day ('Wear Orange'), and honoring Juneteenth 2021.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Items 1–37, Excluding General Business Items 30 and 38)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no pulled items and a registered speaker on Item 1 absent from the queue, Mayor Schewel read the consent agenda spanning board/commission appointments, housing and lead-hazard contracts, water/sewer and stormwater engineering contracts, the FY22 annual insurance plan, and LGC revenue bond application. Council approved the consent agenda unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Development Agreement with Lambert Development Hunt Street II LLC (The Vega / Durham Central Park)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services staffer Robin Parrish and developer attorney Mr. Kuhn presented revisions requested by Council at work session, raising the developer's Affordable Housing Fund contribution from $57,000 to $285,000 ($5,000 per unit) in exchange for Durham Central Park easements and adding resident education materials and non-emergency signage to protect existing park activities like drumming and the skate park. Council praised the enhanced affordable housing proffer and approved all three contract/easement authorizations unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Proposed FY 2021–2022 Budget and FY 2022–2027 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held its final public hearing on the proposed FY22 budget and FY22–27 CIP, hearing roughly 40 speakers on police funding, unarmed mental health crisis responders (Durham for All / Durham Beyond Policing calling to reallocate 60 vacant police positions), ShotSpotter, housing bonds, and employee premium pay. Afterward, Mayor Schewel addressed 2019 housing bond issuance timing and Mark-Anthony Middleton forcefully defended pairing unarmed responders with funded police staffing and ShotSpotter.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (budget vote scheduled June 21)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Plan Amendment — Tier Boundary Change (Industrial Urban to Industrial Suburban)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Alexander Cahill and applicant Dan Jewell (representing existing light-industrial users seeking expansion setbacks and parking flexibility) presented a tier boundary change recommended 12-0 by the Planning Commission. With no public opposition, Council approved the Future Land Use and Tier Boundary Map amendment unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Zoning Map Change — Rollingdale II (602 and 606 W. NC-54 Hwy)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Danny Cultra presented a rezoning request to increase an existing 25-unit townhome approval (PDR 3.940) to 33 townhomes (PDR 5.189), which the Planning Commission had voted 8-4 to deny. Despite neighbor objections led by Ralph Cook and Elizabeth McCain over building height, Jordan Lake watershed stormwater, and density creep—and despite attorney Patrick Byker adding proffers cutting height from 50 to 45 feet, committing to 100-year stormwater treatment, and raising the affordable housing contribution from $25,000 to $33,000—Council passed both the rezoning and consistency statement 5-1 with DeDreana Freeman dissenting.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Second Substantial Amendment to FY20–21 Annual Action Plan / 2020–2025 Consolidated Plan (CARES Act Funding)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and Senior Manager Matthew Schnars presented the second CARES Act substantial amendment allocating the remaining $3,573,901 ($1,513,616 CDBG-CV and $2,260,285 ESG-CV) and reallocating $100,000 from housing counseling to microenterprise business assistance. Speaker Stella Adams opposed shifting funds away from housing counseling ahead of eviction moratorium expiration, while staff explained HUD's strict COVID-nexus timing rules; Council then passed both approval and execution motions 6-0 before entering closed session.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 7, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Rollingdale II Townhome Rezoning (25 to 33 Units) Near Jordan Lake Watershed (Item 41)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 5-1 to override the Planning Commission's 8-4 denial recommendation and approve eight additional townhomes (33 total) at 602–606 W. NC-54 Hwy, with DeDreana Freeman dissenting over watershed, stormwater, and affordability concerns.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the 33-unit townhome rezoning with enhanced proffers (45-ft height cap, 100-year stormwater detention, and $33,000 affordable housing contribution) to add badly needed housing supply and keep units in the low-$300,000 range.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and Mayor Steve Schewel argued Durham faces an acute housing shortage (more realtors than homes for sale) and adding eight units while preserving more open space and buffers benefits the city.

Pierce Freelon noted infrastructure costs spread over 33 units keep prices around $315k–$350k rather than over $400k, and Mark-Anthony Middleton welcomed the amended $33,000 affordable housing and height proffers.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning request in alignment with the Planning Commission's 8-4 vote and neighboring residents' watershed and compatibility objections.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman cited the site's proximity to the Jordan Lake watershed, prior clear-cutting/mass-grading, stormwater and flooding concerns raised by residents, and the fact that $320k–$340k townhomes are not affordable for marginalized residents, noting she was honoring Tom Miller's Planning Commission advice.
disagreements.resolution: Both the rezoning/FLUM ordinance and the consistency statement passed 5-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting Nay.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 7, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: FY22 Policing Budget, Vacant Officer Positions, and ShotSpotter (Public Hearing & Council Response)
disagreements.summary: Following public hearing speakers demanding Council reallocate 60 vacant police officer positions to unarmed crisis responders and reject ShotSpotter, Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton pushed back forcefully in favor of pairing unarmed mental health responders with funded police staffing and gunfire-detection technology.
disagreements.side_a_position: Maintain balanced public safety investments combining unarmed mental health responders with police capacity and ShotSpotter.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton argued residents most affected by gun violence want both unarmed responders and rapid police/lifesaving responses when gunfire occurs, rejecting claims that 'police don't make us safe' or equating ShotSpotter with police killings.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reallocate 60 vacant police officer positions to unarmed responders and community safety programs rather than policing or ShotSpotter.
side_b_arguments: Public hearing speakers (including organizers with Durham for All and Durham Beyond Policing) argued surveys of residents of color favored investing in non-police unarmed responders over vacant police slots.
disagreements.resolution: Public hearing closed with no vote taken; budget adoption remained scheduled for June 21, 2021.

meetings.title: Day 2 - FY22 Council budget work sessions May 27, 2021 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: During Day 2 of the FY 2021-2022 Durham City Council budget work sessions, Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson called the morning session to order before handing the gavel to Mayor Steve Schewel upon his arrival. Council heard departmental budget presentations from outgoing Police Chief Cerelyn Davis—highlighting five cut positions, Axon body-worn and in-car camera contracts, Central Square RMS fee increases, and the national police chief search—alongside a proposal for the new Community Safety Department incorporating alternate response pilots, Bull City United, and $1 million supporting the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force. Afternoon presentations covered Solid Waste yard-waste recovery, Parks and Recreation athletic field maintenance and half-penny property tax funding, and Equity and Inclusion staffing and racial equity tool expansion. At the close of the session, Council gave approval by acclamation to move forward with adding roughly $85,000 for an Immigrant and Refugee Coordinator position.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and BMS/Participatory Budgeting Introduction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson called the special budget work session to order at 9:00 a.m. and turned the chair over to Mayor Steve Schewel upon his arrival. Interim Budget Director John Allore previewed Day 2 department presentations, thanked Budget and Management Services and OPI staff as well as former City Manager Bertha Johnson, and reminded residents that participatory budgeting voting at pbdurham.org remained open through June 6.

agenda_items.title: Durham Police Department FY21-22 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Outgoing Police Chief Cerelyn Davis, joined by incoming Interim Chief Deputy Chief Montgomery and senior command staff, presented DPD's FY21-22 budget, including five position cuts (such as two vacant District 5 motorcycle officer slots) and three budget requests covering Axon body-worn cameras, COBAN-to-Axon in-car camera phase-in, and Central Square RMS maintenance increases. Chief Davis also highlighted the national chief search via Developmental Associates, officer hiring and retention, and 21st-century policing and equity training, while Council thanked her for five years of leadership.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Community Safety Department FY21-22 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Prior to Fire's presentation so Council could consider public safety budgets together, staff presented the proposed new Community Safety Department to advance community-centered prevention and intervention alternatives. The presentation outlined a Community Response Manager structure, small-scale alternate response pilots evaluated by RTI, contractual transfers from DPD (Bull City United and the mental health social worker contract), $100,000 in Bloomberg matching grant IT funds, and $1 million supporting the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force.

agenda_items.title: Solid Waste Operations and Parks & Recreation FY22 Budget Presentations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In the afternoon portion captured in the digest, Solid Waste officials addressed pandemic recovery and resuming yard-waste collection. Parks and Recreation Director Wade Walcutt then presented DPR's FY22 budget, recognizing front-line staff during heightened pandemic park and trail use and explaining capital increases for athletic field maintenance FTEs, heavy equipment, and the half-penny maintenance allocation tied to the proposed two-cent property tax increase.

agenda_items.title: Equity and Inclusion Department FY22 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Director Deborah Giles and Division Manager Sharon Williams presented the Equity and Inclusion Department's budget, maintaining seven General Fund FTEs and requesting one new full-time budget analyst to support contracting/compliance and racial equity initiatives. Highlights included continued funding for the Mayor's Committee for Persons with Disabilities, strategic plan research, employee training, coaching on the racial equity budget evaluation tool, and departmental pilot projects.

agenda_items.title: Council Consensus on $85,000 Immigrant and Refugee Coordinator Allocation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Budget Director John Allore raised a follow-up item from one-on-one Council meetings regarding adding approximately $85,000 for an Immigrant and Refugee Coordinator position. After brief remarks including concurrence from Mark-Anthony Middleton, the chair noted approval by acclamation to move forward with the allocation before adjourning at 1:55 p.m.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Approved by acclamation (no formal roll call)

meetings.title: Day 1 - FY22 Council budget work sessions May 26, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: On Day 1 of the FY 2021-2022 budget work sessions, Council opened by voting 5-0 to excuse Javiera Caballero's travel absence while Charlie Reece connected remotely. Interim Budget Director John Allore presented FY22 revenue forecasts, highlighting 4.14% property tax base growth, stronger-than-expected FY21 sales tax receipts projected at $74.3 million, a proposed FY22 sales tax budget of $76.1 million, and Durham's 16.7% fund balance policy. In the afternoon, the Office of Economic and Workforce Development presented plans to scale Durham YouthWorks tenfold toward nearly 500 youth, expand minority- and women-owned small business technical assistance, and allocate $380,000 for Built to Last and the Durham Compact transition. During that discussion, DeDreana Freeman pressed staff for stronger Council oversight and performance metrics on ongoing operational funding proposed for Made in Durham compared to newer grassroots partners.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call and Excused Absence for Council Member Javiera Caballero
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called Day 1 of the FY22 budget work sessions to order with five members present, Charlie Reece joining via link, and Javiera Caballero absent while traveling. Council voted 5-0 by roll call to excuse Caballero's absence.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Remarks and FY22 Proposed Revenue & Fund Balance Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page thanked budget staff and committed to incorporating Council direction ahead of budget adoption. Interim Budget Director John Allore reported 4.14% tax base growth (68.2% over 10 years), projected FY21 year-end sales tax collections of $74.3 million (up $10 million over the conservative $64.2 million budget), proposed $76.1 million in FY22 sales tax revenue, and discussed Durham's 16.7% minimum fund balance standard.

agenda_items.title: Office of Economic and Workforce Development FY22 Budget and Oversight Questions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD presented its FY22 priorities, including expanding Durham YouthWorks from ~50 virtual participants to nearly 500 youth (ages 14-24), continuing small business capital access and technical assistance ($2.2 million largely supporting minority- and women-owned firms and the African American Legacy cohort), and budgeting $380,000 for Built to Last and the Durham Compact nonprofit transition. DeDreana Freeman questioned moving Made in Durham funding from one-time allocations into ongoing operational support without prior Council review of deliverables and metrics, prompting City Manager Wanda Page to promise scope-of-service details prior to budget adoption.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council May 20, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At its May 20, 2021 virtual work session, all seven Durham City Council members convened before Mark-Anthony Middleton departed early for a prior commitment. DeDreana Freeman announced plans to work with Senator Murdock on a resolution or letter addressing state Critical Race Theory legislation, and City Manager Wanda Page introduced FUSE Fellows Lila Peterson and Dr. Dwayne Campbell alongside priority items including emergency RDU Airport CARES/CRRSA grant items requiring rule suspension before June 1. Council reviewed consent items ranging from board gender-balance bylaws and homelessness diversion to water/sewer infrastructure and utility revenue bonds, then received an extensive Greater Triangle Commuter Rail feasibility briefing estimating $1.8 billion to $2.1 billion in capital costs and analyzing affordable housing along the corridor. Council closed by reading board nominations and voting 6-0 (with Middleton having departed early) to settle the June regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Schedule Adjustments, and Critical Race Theory Bill Response
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the work session to order with all seven members present and noted Mark-Anthony Middleton would leave early. During announcements, DeDreana Freeman stated she was working with Senator Murdock on a resolution or statement regarding pending Critical Race Theory legislation in the NC House, and Mayor Schewel suggested a rapid sign-on letter if the bill advanced quickly.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items, FUSE Fellows Introduction, and RDU FAA Grants
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented priority items including two supplemental USDOT/FAA Coronavirus Response Grant Program items for RDU Airport requiring suspension of rules for same-day action ahead of a June 1 deadline, updates on the FY21 budget amendment (Item 12), Q3 financial report (Item 28), and Hunt Street development agreement (Item 30), plus one citizen matter. She also introduced FUSE Fellows Lila Peterson and Dr. Dwayne Campbell, who will support the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force and proposed Community Safety Department.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Motion moved and seconded; roll call truncated in digest

agenda_items.title: Review of Board Appointments, Community Development, and Infrastructure Consent Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed Items 8 through 31, flagging board/commission gender-balance bylaws compliance, confirming Ward 3 residency for an appointee, praising Volunteers of America Carolinas homelessness diversion outcomes (Item 13), and discussing Habitat for Humanity minor home repair (Item 14). Members also reviewed Water Management lift station, roof, waterline, and biosolids contracts (Items 20-26), FY22 insurance, Q3 financials (Item 28), and pulled Item 29 (utility system revenue bond LGC application).

agenda_items.title: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Feasibility Study Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: GoTriangle and Triangle J Council of Governments staff presented the Greater Triangle Commuter Rail feasibility update, citing year-of-expenditure capital estimates of $1.8 billion (to Garner/shorter corridor) to $2.1 billion (to Clayton), downtown Durham track and utility engineering with Kimley-Horn, and survey results showing 87% positive sentiment led by frequency, reliability, accessibility, and affordability. TJCOG reported that 37% of legally binding affordable homes are within one mile of the corridor and projected that figure would nearly double over 10 years, while Council pressed staff on post-COVID remote-work ridership projections and fare capping so fares do not price out current bus riders.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations Report and Settling the Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk announced board nominations including Ingrid Poll (Ward 2), Anita A. Daniels-Kinney (Ward 3), and Jen Fry (Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee). City Manager Wanda Page presented the settled agenda, and Council voted 6-0 (with Mark-Anthony Middleton having departed early) to approve it before adjourning at 4:24 p.m.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council May 17, 2021 at 7 p.m.
meetings.executive_summary: At its May 17, 2021 regular virtual meeting, all seven members of the Durham City Council recognized the Durham Recovery and Renewal Task Force co-chairs and issued proclamations for Period Poverty Awareness Week and Tourette's Syndrome Awareness Day. Following public hearings, Council unanimously passed three 7-0 votes approving a Suburban-to-Urban Tier Comprehensive Plan amendment, RU-5(D) rezoning, and consistency statement, followed by three 7-0 votes authorizing a new five-year Downtown Durham Municipal Service District contract with Downtown Durham, Inc. (up to $1,181,500 in year one). Council also voted 7-0 to adopt revised FY 2022 stormwater rates effective July 1, 2021, raising residential Tier 1, 2, and 3 monthly fees by $0.25, $0.51, and $3.00 respectively.

agenda_items.title: Recovery & Renewal Task Force Recognition, Proclamations, and Vaccine Updates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council honored Durham Recovery and Renewal Task Force co-chairs Matisha Sims and Katie Galbraith, proclaimed Period Poverty Awareness Week with Diaper Bank of NC Executive Director Michelle Old, and proclaimed June 4 as Tourette's Syndrome Awareness Day with Chelsea Phoebeach. During announcements, Javiera Caballero shared walk-in COVID-19 vaccine access for ages 12+ at Wheels and Duke's Karsh Alumni Center, and members noted an Office of Equity and Inclusion FUSE fellowship.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Tier Amendment (Suburban to Urban) and RU-5(D) Zoning Map Change
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Closing the public hearing with support expressed for the proposed development, Council approved three consecutive motions—amending the Comprehensive Plan Tier Map and Future Land Use Map from Suburban to Urban Tier, rezoning the property from RS-20 and RU-5 to RU-5 with a development plan, and adopting the consistency statement—each passing 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Five-Year Contract with Downtown Durham, Inc. for Downtown Durham Municipal Service District
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff member Mr. Nixon and Downtown Durham, Inc. President Nicole Thompson appeared for the public hearing on renewing DDI's management of the Downtown Durham Municipal Service District, with no public speakers signed up. Council unanimously approved three motions authorizing a five-year contract (July 1, 2021 through June 30, 2026), year-one funding up to $1,181,500, and future payments subject to budget authorization.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Ordinance Revising FY 2022 Stormwater Fee Schedule
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staffer Paul Wiebke presented the proposed FY 2022 stormwater rate adjustments effective July 1, 2021 ($0.25/month increase to $3.75 for Tier 1, $0.51/month to $7.76 for Tier 2, $3.00/month for Tier 3 residential, and $0.51 per 2,400 sq. ft. impervious surface for non-residential). After DeDreana Freeman praised staff's creative rate structuring and no public speakers appeared, Council unanimously adopted the ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Resolution Amending Comprehensive Plan Tier Map and FLUM (Suburban Tier to Urban Tier)
votes.discussion_detail: Following the closed public hearing, Charlie Reece moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the resolution amending the Comprehensive Plan Tier Map and Future Land Use Map from Suburban Tier to Urban Tier; the motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Adopt UDO Ordinance Rezoning Property from RS-20 and RU-5 to RU-5(D)
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the UDO rezoning ordinance taking the property out of RS-20 and RU-5 and establishing RU-5 with a development plan; the motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consistency Statement for RU-5(D) Zoning Map Change
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement; the motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Item 30 — Authorize Five-Year Contract with Downtown Durham, Inc. (FY22-FY26)
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded authorizing the City Manager to execute a five-year contract with Downtown Durham, Inc. (July 1, 2021 to June 30, 2026) to operate the Downtown Durham Municipal Service District; all seven members voted Aye.

votes.item_title: Item 30 — Authorize Year-One MSD Payment to Downtown Durham, Inc. (Up to $1,181,500)
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded authorizing payment to Downtown Durham, Inc. up to $1,181,500 for the first fiscal year of the MSD contract; the motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Item 30 — Authorize Future MSD Payments Subject to Budget Authorization
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded authorizing future MSD contract payments subject to annual City Council budget authorization; all seven members voted Aye.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Revising FY 2022 Stormwater Fee Schedule
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the ordinance revising the stormwater fee schedule effective July 1, 2021; the motion passed unanimously 7-0.

meetings.title: City Manager Wanda Page's FY 2021 - 2022 Budget Presentation May 17, 2021
meetings.executive_summary: In her inaugural budget address on May 17, 2021, City Manager Wanda Page presented a proposed $524.6 million FY 2021-2022 budget (a 4.38% increase) and a $235.6 million General Fund budget (up 9.8%), utilizing $10.2 million in fund balance alongside a proposed two-cent property tax rate increase to 55.176 cents per $100 of assessed value. Page allocated 1.38 cents of the tax hike to debt service for the $95 million 2019 Affordable Housing Bond ($12.7 million dedicated housing budget, plus $500,000 for a longtime homeowner tax grant), 0.5 cents to green and equitable infrastructure debt service, and 0.12 cents to the General Fund, while proposing a new Community Safety Department to lead non-police crisis prevention and intervention and staff the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force. All seven City Council members warmly praised the proposal ahead of budget work sessions and hearings, while Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman noted they would continue probing details to ensure equitable staffing and responsiveness to marginalized residents; no votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Wanda Page's FY 2021-2022 Proposed Budget and CIP Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page outlined a $524.6 million total budget ($235.6 million General Fund) funded in part by $10.2 million in fund balance and a proposed two-cent property tax increase (1.38 cents for Affordable Housing Bond debt, 0.5 cents for green and equitable infrastructure, and 0.12 cents for General Fund operations), plus previously discussed water, stormwater, solid waste, and planning fee updates. Key initiatives included creating the Community Safety Department, expanding Forever Home Durham to $12.7 million for FY22 (including Willard Street Apartments and a $500,000 longtime homeowner tax grant for <=30% AMI residents), employee pay increases, and COVID-19 recovery.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Comments on Proposed Budget Priorities
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After confirming registered public speaker Hillary Ensminger was not present in the virtual queue, all seven Council members expressed strong enthusiasm for Page's first budget. Members highlighted full housing bond funding, the Community Safety Department, the language access coordinator, green and equitable infrastructure, the Office on Performance and Innovation, and future transit fare considerations, while Middleton and Freeman emphasized testing the budget's impact on marginalized communities and departmental staffing needs during upcoming work sessions.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting with Congressman David Price (NC 4th District) May 10, 2021
meetings.executive_summary: Durham City Council held a 45-minute special virtual meeting with U.S. Representative David Price (NC-04) and senior staffer Tracy Lovett, moderated by Senior Assistant to the City Manager Karmisha Wallace, to align local priorities with federal appropriations and COVID-19 relief opportunities. City leaders thanked Price for his 34 years of service, light-rail advocacy, CDBG support, and CARES Act rent and utility assistance, while Price highlighted the return of transparent congressional community project funding (earmarks), HUD Section 811 and Choice Neighborhoods grants, and federal Treasury relief monitoring alongside Durham's $95 million affordable housing bond. During Q&A, Council members questioned Price on H.R. 40 reparations legislation, addressing decades of deferred maintenance in public housing communities like McDougald Terrace through federal infrastructure bills, alternative community safety responses, federal voting rights (H.R. 1) amid the Senate filibuster, and immigration and refugee policy; no formal votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Durham City Priorities Overview and Congressman David Price Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel and Karmisha Wallace welcomed Congressman David Price, thanking him for supporting the American Tobacco Trail, prior light-rail efforts, CDBG funding, and CARES Act rental/utility relief administered with Durham County Social Services. Price outlined opportunities from the return of transparent congressional earmarks, pairing federal housing programs (Section 811, Choice Neighborhoods) with Durham's $95 million affordable housing bond to counter gentrification, and tracking nearly $2 trillion in federal relief.

agenda_items.title: Dialogue on Public Housing Maintenance, Policing Alternatives, Voting Rights, and Immigration
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Congressman Price responded to Council questions regarding his co-sponsorship of H.R. 40 on reparations, efforts to fold public housing deferred-maintenance backlogs (such as McDougald Terrace) into federal infrastructure legislation, and support for flexible alternatives to traditional policing. Jillian Johnson pressed Price on passing federal voting rights legislation (H.R. 1) against state-level voter suppression given the Senate filibuster, and Council also discussed immigration and refugee reforms; Price noted budget reconciliation bypasses the filibuster for relief and infrastructure, whereas voting and immigration bills face the filibuster directly.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council May 6, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Presiding from City Hall for the first time during a work session with all seven members virtual, Mayor Steve Schewel opened the May 6, 2021 meeting with condolences for Deputy City Manager Keith Chadwell following the loss of his wife Jocelyn. Council accepted City Manager Wanda Page's priority items—including EPA Brownfields work, a 2021 pavement condition survey, and a supplemental Vaccine Equity Proposal—and reviewed an extensive slate of items covering temporary outdoor dining extensions, Fidelity's land donation for Fire Station 19 (saving an estimated $1.6 million), Durham Bulls Athletic Park design-build contracts, and the Downtown Durham Municipal Service District renewal. Public Works presented an FY22-25 stormwater rate model to support peaking capital projects and Falls/Jordan Lake rules, and Mayor Schewel outlined a five-month city-county cost-shared vaccine equity proposal to embed additional community health workers in local CBOs, prompting DeDreana Freeman to ask how mid-year emergency proposals fit within the standard budget process. Council closed by receiving board nomination tallies and voting 7-0 to settle the regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Announcements and City Manager Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel offered condolences to Deputy City Manager Keith Chadwell on the passing of his wife Jocelyn. City Manager Wanda Page presented five priority items—updated attachments for EPA Brownfields (Item 18) and Pavement Condition Survey ST-314 (Item 20), moving the Downtown MSD annual report (Item 26) to departmental items, a stormwater rate presentation (Item 31), and supplemental Item 32 (Vaccine Equity Proposal)—and Council took a roll call vote on a motion by Pierce Freelon and Jillian Johnson to accept them.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (Roll Call; partial votes in digest gap)

agenda_items.title: Consent Review, Resident Complaint, and Temporary Outdoor Seating Extension
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed Items 5 through 32, pulling Item 7 (temporary outdoor seating ordinance extension) and Item 14 (Dewberry Design Builders contract for Durham Bulls Athletic Park), while noting Fidelity's land donation for Fire Station 19 saving ~$1.6 million (Item 15) and EPA Brownfields history (Item 18). After hearing resident Cheryl Datsaba's neighborhood cleanup complaint, Council discussed Item 7, with Mayor Schewel requesting an October report from staff and DDI on permanent outdoor dining rules and another member preferring parking-space use over public parks.

agenda_items.title: FY 2022 Stormwater Funding and Rate Model Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staffer Paul Wiebke presented the $11.6 million Stormwater enterprise fund (104 FTEs), detailing the FY22-25 rate model designed to support peak capital spending in FY22-23 and comply with NPDES permits and Jordan/Falls Lake nutrient rules ahead of the May 17 public hearing.

agenda_items.title: COVID-19 Vaccine Equity Community Health Worker Proposal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presented a five-month city-county cost-sharing proposal developed with community organizations, Public Health Director Rod Jenkins, Lincoln Community Health Center, and Duke/Gillings partners to deploy additional community health workers and health ambassadors. DeDreana Freeman expressed support while asking Wanda Page and staff how mid-year emergency funding requests are accommodated outside normal budget submissions, and Javiera Caballero asked about the County Commission's timeline.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations Report, Settle Regular Meeting Agenda, and DOST Bylaws Follow-up
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk announced board nomination vote counts, and Council voted 7-0 to settle the regular meeting agenda (Consent Items 1-22, 26, and 32; GBA Item 23; GBA public hearings Items 28-31). Javiera Caballero and DeDreana Freeman agreed to follow up with Open Space and Trails (DOST) representatives regarding a full bylaws rewrite before adjourning at 6:14 p.m.
