meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept 24, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting virtually on September 24, 2020, all seven Durham City Council members welcomed Deputy City Manager Wanda Page ahead of her October 1 transition to Interim City Manager and approved her priority agenda items 7-0. During an extensive five-and-a-half-hour work session, Council received presentations on the Cities Addressing Fines and Fees Equitably (CAFE) water cutoff equity study, staff updates on the Duke Energy franchise and Clean Energy MOU following public comment, southeastern Durham (SEARLS/Searles Basin) land use and sewer infrastructure challenges, Participatory Budgeting Cycle 2's proposed $1 million shift toward COVID-related nonprofit grants, the Move Durham transportation vision plan, and a $77 million FY 2021 Capital Improvement Plan prioritizing core maintenance and $10 million in street paving. Council members debated the 10-year vs. 7-year Duke Energy franchise term and how to weigh suburban road and transit deficits against pending southeastern Durham annexations without creating a de facto moratorium, then refined Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson's federal advocacy resolution and committee structure for Racial Equity Task Force recommendations. Council concluded by advancing board nominations, settling the next regular meeting agenda 7-0, and voting 7-0 to enter closed session on a real estate transaction.

agenda_items.title: Council Remarks on Gun Violence Prevention, Violence Interrupters, and Racial Equity Task Force
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members opened with reflections on recent community gun violence, noting upcoming work on violence interruption and the Safety and Wellness Task Force. Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson previewed her draft resolution and subcommittees to advance Racial Equity Task Force recommendations, while Council Member DeDreana Freeman urged sustained urgency on community-led violence prevention.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items (Wanda Page)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Incoming Interim City Manager Wanda Page presented five priority items: updated attachment 2 for Item 6 (FY 2021 Participatory Budgeting), new attachment 3 for Item 11 (High Pressure Zone Improvements), early scheduling for Item 24 (CAFE fines and fees update), attachments 7-9 for Item 27 (Duke Energy franchise), and supplemental Item 34 (Consolidated Annexation — Sykes Property). DeDreana Freeman moved and Jillian Johnson seconded approval.

agenda_items.title: Administrative Consent Agenda Review and Legislative Agenda Requests
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed consent items 1 through 23, with Charlie Reece thanking Audit Services for the water meter billing audit (Item 4), noting Item 1 had a single strong applicant for the Human Relations Commission, and urging staff to respond to Durham CAN's comments on 505 West Chapel Hill Street (Item 18). DeDreana Freeman requested adding the municipal cost of storing confiscated firearms that state law prevents destroying (raised by Item 19) to the City's legislative agenda.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment on Gunfire Safety and Duke Energy Clean Energy MOU
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Heath Knight recounted a September 4 incident in which a rifle bullet entered her living room and urged Council to communicate more transparently and act urgently on violent crime. Casey Collins of the Environmental Affairs Board urged Council to ensure the Duke Energy Clean Energy MOU reflects community-wide climate and renewable energy goals rather than city operations alone.

agenda_items.title: Update on Cities Addressing Fines and Fees Equitably (CAFE) Water Utility Initiative
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Ryan Smith, Duke researcher Michael Daly, Utility Finance Manager Heidi Hackett, and National League of Cities specialist Courtney Coffin presented data showing 750,000 late fees and 36,000+ $50 water disconnection fees over three years disproportionately burdened lower-income and Black census tracts. Staff reported nearly exhausting the $150,000 online Water Hardship Fund, redesigned disconnect notices, prepared the Lift Up debt-elimination coaching pilot, and proposed eliminating the $50 disconnection fee (offset by roughly $0.50/month across customer bills).

agenda_items.title: Duke Energy Carolinas LLC Franchise Agreement, Operating Agreement, and Clean Energy MOU Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson and General Services staff Stacy Poston responded to September 21 public hearing feedback and Environmental Affairs Board (EAB) edits, maintaining the proposed 10-year franchise term while negotiating EAB clean-energy revisions into the living MOU and preparing an October 1 Green Source Advantage solar RFI. Charlie Reece questioned whether a 7-year term would better preserve agility amid rapid energy shifts, while Mark-Anthony Middleton and Bo Ferguson argued the living MOU and statutory limits made 10 years reasonable, with Steve Schewel preferring 7 years but willing to accept 10.

agenda_items.title: Land Use and Infrastructure Issues in Southeastern Durham (SEARLS / Searles Basin)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Sara Young, Water Management's Don Greeley, and Transportation's Bill Judge briefed Council on 2,500+ approved and 3,700+ proposed residential units in southeastern Durham, extensive stream/floodplain/wildlife corridor constraints, the $48.5 million Searles lift station and gravity sewer project (35% complete, $5,437/unit basin fee), and narrow state farm-to-market roads. Council members weighed concerns about approving dense suburban subdivisions ahead of transit and road upgrades against Mark-Anthony Middleton's and Steve Schewel's caution that delaying or denying compliant proposals without UDO/Comprehensive Plan changes risked appearing arbitrary or creating a de facto moratorium.

agenda_items.title: FY 2021 Participatory Budgeting (PB) Process Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Engagement Manager Andrew Holland, Robin Baker, and PB Steering Committee member Sarah Ma reviewed Cycle 1 diversity metrics and proposed pivoting Cycle 2 from capital projects to $1 million in nonprofit relief grants (up to $50,000 each) targeting pandemic-exacerbated community needs such as food insecurity and unemployment. Council members praised the shift and queried outreach equity, Spanish-language access, grant size, and the May 2021-to-July 2021 disbursement schedule.

agenda_items.title: Move Durham Transportation Study Final Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation planner Ellen Beckman presented the final Move Durham vision plan for central Durham, prioritizing people over vehicle throughput, two-way street conversions, transit priority corridors on Holloway and Fayetteville streets, Vision Zero speed management, and equitable re-evaluation of NC 147 with NCDOT. Council and staff noted that sidewalk funding in the CIP ends after FY 2023 and discussed pursuing a local transportation bond or dedicated funding alongside regional and state dollars.

agenda_items.title: FY 2021 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director David Boyd and Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson presented the $77 million FY 2021 general-fund CIP, emphasizing core infrastructure maintenance after shifting $5 million to the City COVID Relief Fund. Staff highlighted restoring $4 million from CIP capacity to preserve the full $10 million street paving budget and noted that the 10-year model has no remaining debt capacity through FY 2026, with formal appropriation ordinances scheduled for the next council cycle.

agenda_items.title: Racial Equity Task Force Implementation Plan and Federal Advocacy Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson outlined a phased plan for 12 Racial Equity Task Force recommendations, including a federal advocacy resolution supporting reparations, universal basic income, a federal jobs guarantee, and a higher federal minimum wage (which she agreed to broaden beyond $15/hour per DeDreana Freeman's living-wage feedback). Council endorsed placing cannabis decriminalization and civilian review board subpoena power on the state legislative agenda, forming history/storytelling and cemetery subcommittees under existing boards with Pierce Freelon consulting, and asking the City Attorney to draft bylaws for a permanent Race Equity Commission.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations, Agenda Setting, and Closed Session on Real Estate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Clerk reported Fara Campbell received four votes for the Human Relations Commission, and DeDreana Freeman changed her vote to give Brenna Casey a four-vote majority for the Mayor's Council for Women. Council then unanimously settled the October 5 regular meeting agenda and voted 7-0 to enter closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(5) regarding a real estate transaction.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager Priority Items
votes.notes: Mayor Schewel noted Jillian Johnson was initially muted during the roll call before confirming her Aye vote.
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Jillian Johnson seconded approval of City Manager Wanda Page's five priority agenda additions and scheduling requests. All seven council members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Settle Regular City Council Meeting Agenda
votes.discussion_detail: Javiera Caballero moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded settling the upcoming City Council meeting agenda with Consent Items 1-23 and General Business Agenda Public Hearings Items 27-31 and Item 34. All seven members voted Aye.

votes.item_title: Adjourn to Closed Session for Real Estate Transaction (NCGS 143-318.11(a)(5))
votes.discussion_detail: At the City Attorney's guidance to consider a real estate transaction under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(5), DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded entering closed session. All seven members voted Aye.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept 24, 2020 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Duke Energy Franchise Agreement Term Length (7 Years vs. 10 Years)
disagreements.summary: Council members and staff debated whether to shorten the proposed 10-year Duke Energy electric franchise term to 7 years (as recommended by the Environmental Affairs Board) to maintain flexibility amid rapid renewable energy and regulatory changes.
disagreements.side_a_position: Favor a shorter 7-year term to avoid locking the City into outdated terms as clean energy technology and state policy evolve.
side_a_arguments: Rapid technological, regulatory, and legislative shifts in electricity generation and resale make a shorter term prudent.
The Environmental Affairs Board recommended no more than 7 years to keep leverage aligned with community climate goals.
disagreements.side_b_position: Retain the 10-year franchise term because right-of-way rules are standard while clean-energy goals live in the flexible MOU.
side_b_arguments: Under NC law and utilities commission jurisdiction, the franchise only governs right-of-way poles and wires, whereas the Clean Energy MOU is a living, biennial work-plan document.
Seven years versus 10 years is arbitrary without an identified missed opportunity, and 10 years is already shorter than prior 15- to 20-year franchises.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken at the work session; Steve Schewel indicated he preferred 7 years but could live with 10 years while directing staff to finalize EAB-suggested edits to the MOU before the October 5 vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept 24, 2020 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Evaluating Pending Southeastern Durham Annexations Amid Infrastructure Deficits
disagreements.summary: Following the SEARLS/Searles Basin briefing showing 3,700+ proposed residential units alongside strained two-lane state roads and limited transit, Council members diverged on whether to hold back pending suburban annexations or avoid changing expectations mid-review.
disagreements.side_a_position: Scrutinize or pause approvals of dense car-dependent developments in southeastern Durham until transit, road, and small-area planning gaps are addressed.
side_a_arguments: Approving thousands more residential units along unmodernized two-lane roads without transit locks in unsustainable growth before comprehensive planning catches up.
Council must avoid repeatedly approving incremental developments that strain infrastructure and fail to match urban infill priorities.
disagreements.side_b_position: Do not impose an uncodified de facto moratorium on compliant projects; instead codify any policy shifts in the UDO or Comprehensive Plan.
side_b_arguments: Changing rules mid-game after developers pay fees and follow existing plans risks appearing capricious and harms city credibility.
Adjoining Wake County growth shows that rejecting city-utility projects can push development onto large-lot septic systems in clay soils, worsening environmental risk.
disagreements.resolution: Informational work-session discussion; staff was asked to brief absent members Javiera Caballero and DeDreana Freeman ahead of the October 5 public hearings on continued cases.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Sept 21, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: In the live-stream recording of the September 21, 2020 virtual regular meeting, all seven Durham City Council members opened with a moment of silence for Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg and nearly an hour of farewell tributes to retiring City Manager Tom Bonfield, including establishing an annual Tom Bonfield Scholarship at Durham Technical Community College. Council approved the Consent Agenda 7-0 and held a public hearing on the 10-year Duke Energy franchise renewal, operating agreement, and Clean Energy MOU—where speakers and Environmental Affairs Board representatives urged a 7-year term, expanded municipal clean-energy rights, and fixes for glaring 4,000K LED streetlights—continuing the hearing to September 24 and October 5. Council unanimously approved 7-0 the NC Highway 55 ABC Store annexation and zoning translation, continued the 80-unit Sykes Property annexation to October 5 pending the southeastern Durham infrastructure briefing, and voted 7-0 to adopt UDO Text Amendment TC2000003 governing statutory development agreements after extensive debate over equity guardrails.

agenda_items.title: Moment of Silence for Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Tributes to Retiring City Manager Tom Bonfield
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel led a moment of silence for the late Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg before former Mayors Bill Bell and Cora Cole-McFadden, Bill Kalkhof, Anthony Scott, Farad Ali, Senator Mike Woodard, and council colleagues honored retiring City Manager Tom Bonfield's 12-year tenure. Schewel also announced the Tom Bonfield Scholarship at Durham Technical Community College for university transfer students interested in government or policy.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations for National Preparedness Month and Diaper Need Awareness Week, Plus Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel proclaimed September 2020 National Preparedness Month and September 21-27 Diaper Need Awareness Week. Council members discussed flu shots and the 2020 Census (Charlie Reece), self-limiting speeches to five minutes and seeking a pause on LED streetlight replacements (Reece and Javiera Caballero), Hispanic Heritage Month (Caballero), youth gun violence and BLAST outreach (Mark-Anthony Middleton, Pierce Freelon, DeDreana Freeman), and transit rides to polling sites (Freelon and Freeman).

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items and Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield recognized the passing of Solid Waste employee Donald Kimbro, presented updated materials for Items 11 and 18, and moved Item 26 (Duke Energy franchise) to the first public hearing. Council approved Consent Items 1-5, 7-9, 11-14, and 27 unanimously 7-0 on roll call.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Duke Energy Carolinas LLC Franchise Renewal, Operating Agreement, Clean Energy MOU, and LED Streetlights
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson introduced the proposed franchise renewal, operating agreement, and Clean Energy MOU, followed by 12 community speakers split between institutional/nonprofit partners praising Duke Energy's grants and EAB/resident advocates calling for a 7-year term, renewable power authority, and relief from unshielded 4,000K LED streetlights. Transportation Assistant Director Bill Judge reported 18,671 of 21,000 LED conversions completed and 95 complaints (64 resolved via $100 shields), and Council continued the public hearing open to the September 24 work session and October 5 meeting.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Consolidated Annexation: NC Highway 55 ABC Store (5608 & 5612 NC 55 Hwy)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Emily Struthers presented the 11.97-acre voluntary annexation, utility extension agreement, and exact zoning translation for 5608 and 5612 NC 55 Highway, with applicant Andrew Porter speaking in support. With no opposition, Council approved the annexation/UEA ordinance, consistency statement, and zoning map ordinance 7-0 across three roll call votes.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Consolidated Annexation: Sykes Property (7008 & 7012 Leesville Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Grace Smith presented the 40.36-acre annexation and exact Rural Residential zoning translation for an 80-lot single-family conservation subdivision preserving 20 acres of open space, with applicant attorney Nil Ghosh, Erica Leatham (M/I Homes), and Bob Zumwalt answering questions on traffic, price points, and lack of administrative design commitments. At the request of DeDreana Freeman and Jillian Johnson to await the September 24 southeastern Durham briefing, the applicant agreed to continue the hearing to October 5.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Unified Development Ordinance Text Amendment: Development Agreements (TC2000003)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Michael Stock and Assistant City Attorney Don O'Toole presented TC2000003 establishing local UDO rules for statutory development agreements under NCGS 160D-1001, incorporating revised Attachment C to clarify Planning Commission three-cycle continuance authority and environmental protections. Following support from affordable housing developers (DHIC and Laurel Street) and opposition from Ellen Plass and Katie Rose Levin citing the Planning Commission's 4-10 denial vote, Council debated transparency and housing benefits before adopting the consistency statement and text amendment 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 17 — Adopt Ordinance Annexing NC Highway 55 ABC Store and Entering Utility Extension Agreement
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman's name was omitted in the transcript audio of the first roll call, though the clerk confirmed unanimous 7-0 passage and Freeman voted Aye on the immediately following two votes.
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting the annexation ordinance and utility extension agreement for 5608 and 5612 NC 55 Highway. Mayor Schewel announced unanimous passage.

votes.item_title: Item 17 — Adopt Consistency Statement for NC Highway 55 ABC Store Zoning Map Change
votes.discussion_detail: Jillian Johnson moved and Charlie Reece seconded adopting the Comprehensive Plan consistency statement for the NC Highway 55 ABC Store zoning translation. All seven members voted Aye.

votes.item_title: Item 17 — Adopt Ordinance Amending Zoning Map for NC Highway 55 ABC Store
votes.discussion_detail: Jillian Johnson moved and Pierce Freelon seconded adopting the zoning map ordinance for the NC Highway 55 ABC Store parcels. All seven members voted Aye.

votes.item_title: Item 19 — Adopt Consistency Statement for UDO Text Amendment TC2000003 (Development Agreements)
votes.notes: Individual mover and seconder names were not announced aloud before the roll call.
votes.discussion_detail: Council moved and seconded adopting the Comprehensive Plan consistency statement for UDO Text Amendment TC2000003. All seven members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Item 19 — Adopt Ordinance Amending UDO for Statutory Development Agreements (TC2000003)
votes.notes: Mayor Schewel initially misidentified Pierce Freelon as seconder before correcting it to Mark-Anthony Middleton at 04:40:21.
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the revised Attachment C ordinance amending the UDO for statutory development agreements. All seven members voted Aye on roll call.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Sept 21, 2020 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Guardrails, Scope, and Community Access in UDO Text Amendment TC2000003 (Development Agreements)
disagreements.summary: While Council adopted TC2000003 unanimously 7-0, members and public speakers clashed over whether statutory development agreements lacked sufficient public-access guardrails or represented an essential local tool for affordable housing.
disagreements.side_a_position: The draft text amendment risks creating a separate, developer-favored process where complex 40-page contracts are negotiated before public notice and not limited solely to affordable housing.
side_a_arguments: The Planning Commission recommended denial 4-10, warning of expedited hearing risks, insufficient early neighborhood engagement, and unrestricted non-housing uses.
Residents in rapidly gentrifying neighborhoods like Walltown and Braggtown face barriers reviewing 40-page legal contracts late in the process.
disagreements.side_b_position: Development agreements already exist under state law, and TC2000003 adds stronger local guardrails while unlocking affordable housing tools unavailable through standard zoning.
side_b_arguments: Durham's affordable housing density bonus has gone unused, whereas development agreements enable projects like Laurel Street's Farrington Road mixed-income development.
TC2000003 exceeds state law by requiring neighborhood meetings, Planning Commission review with three-cycle continuances, and zero weakening of environmental protections.
disagreements.resolution: Following the inclusion of Planning Commission continuance protections in revised Attachment C, Council voted 7-0 to adopt both the consistency statement and ordinance at 04:41:00.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept 10, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Welcoming newly seated Ward 3 Council Member Pierce Freelon to his first work session on September 10, 2020, the Durham City Council passed City Manager Tom Bonfield's priority items 7-0 and approved 7-0 City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg's request for a closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(1) to view law enforcement body-camera recordings from an August 21 incident at Rochelle Manor. During Citizens' Matters, speakers addressed Engaged Durham transparency and urged downzoning of the Black Meadow Ridge parcels near West Point on the Eno, while Council questioned staff on pulled consent items—notably Pierce Freelon and Charlie Reece pressing Transportation Director Sean Egan over equity review and local contracting in the $100,000 Texas A&M Transportation Institute contract. Following an FY 2020 Q4 financial briefing, a 6-month free ShotSpotter pilot presentation sparked sharp philosophical disagreement—with Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman urging the free trial to confront neighborhood gunfire, while Jillian Johnson, Pierce Freelon, Charlie Reece, and Javiera Caballero opposed expanding armed police responses and surveillance in favor of non-police crisis and violence-interruption models—ending without a motion. Council also reviewed the proposed 10-year Duke Energy franchise and Clean Energy MOU, discussed selecting a city manager search firm, nominated board appointees (including Courtney James to the Affordable Housing Implementation Committee), and voted 6-0 (Jillian Johnson absent) to settle the September 21 agenda.

agenda_items.title: Welcome to Pierce Freelon, Announcements, City Manager and City Attorney Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel welcomed Pierce Freelon to his first work session, and Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson requested time at the September 24 work session to present Racial Equity Task Force implementation resolutions. Council voted 7-0 to approve City Manager Tom Bonfield's priority items (referring Item 10 back to administration and adding Duke Energy, Shannon Road culvert, and city manager search firm findings) and voted 7-0 to approve City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg's closed session request to view court-ordered law enforcement recordings.

agenda_items.title: Administrative Consent Review and Pulled Items (Items 2, 6, 9, and 11)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council referred Item 6 (DHA appointment) back to the Clerk and pulled Items 2, 9, and 11 for discussion. On Item 9 (Longtime Homeowner Tax Deferment Program), Tom Bonfield clarified for DeDreana Freeman that the existing neighborhood grant program remained in a fourth pilot year alongside the new countywide 30% AMI deferral program; on Item 11 (Texas A&M Transportation Institute $100,000 contract), Charlie Reece and Pierce Freelon pressed Transportation Director Sean Egan to clarify GoDurham rider stakeholder inclusion, obtain TTI workforce demographics, and consider local minority-owned firms for future communications work.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment on Engaged Durham Transparency and Black Meadow Ridge Zoning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Ellen Plass criticized the omission of top-ranked public concerns such as government accountability and displacement from recent Engaged Durham Comprehensive Plan materials. Four speakers—Ariane Cheek, Christina Benson, Nancy Cox, and Jessica Sheffield (Eno River Association)—urged Council to proactively initiate downzoning of the 50-acre Black Meadow Ridge parcels adjacent to West Point on the Eno after a Planning Director memo noted no valid development plan exists for its PDR 6.2 designation.

agenda_items.title: FY 2019-20 Fourth Quarter Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant Budget Director John Allore and Finance Director David Boyd briefed Council on FY 2020 year-end financials, noting spending reductions cushioned initial COVID-19 revenue losses while warning that FY 2021 will bring sharper revenue impacts for DPAC, Durham Bulls Athletic Park, and uncollectible water bills during the cutoff moratorium. Council also discussed timing for issuing the 2019 affordable housing bond debt (projected for late calendar year 2021) and potential COVID relief funding for utility hardship.

agenda_items.title: ShotSpotter Acoustic Gunshot Detection Six-Month Pilot Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Cerelyn Davis and ShotSpotter consultant Ron Teachman presented a proposed no-cost, six-month pilot covering three square miles ($210,000/year if later adopted) to detect unreported gunfire within 60 seconds. Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman argued urgently for testing the free pilot to protect children and residents living with nightly gunfire, while Jillian Johnson, Pierce Freelon, Charlie Reece, and Javiera Caballero opposed the technology over false positives, expanded armed police presence, surveillance concerns, and a desire to prioritize violence interrupters and unarmed crisis response; no motion was offered and the item remained with administration.

agenda_items.title: Duke Energy Carolinas LLC Franchise Agreement, Operating Agreement, and Clean Energy MOU Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson, Assistant City Attorney Don O'Toole, and Stacy Poston presented the proposed 10-year franchise agreement, operational relocation/tree-trimming agreement, and first-ever Clean Energy MOU ahead of the September 21 public hearing. Staff explained that NC Utilities Commission authority limits municipal franchises to right-of-way regulation while the franchise appendix reserves the City's right to generate and store power if state law permits, and the MOU establishes a joint work plan for EV infrastructure, Green Source Advantage solar, and energy efficiency.

agenda_items.title: Human Resources Briefing on Executive Search Firms and Selection Timeline
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR Director Regina Youngblood presented profiles of eight executive search firms and outlined a 2-to-3-week selection process followed by a 90-to-120-day recruitment. Council members Javiera Caballero and DeDreana Freeman requested candidate-of-color placement metrics and RFP/workforce comparisons, while Mark-Anthony Middleton and Steve Schewel emphasized taking adequate time under Incoming Interim Manager Wanda Page to gather public input and update the job description.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations, Agenda Settling, and Closed Session Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council finalized board nominations—re-advertising Carolina Theatre, recommending Chastin Swain (EAB), Harold Frisco (Homeless Services), and adding Courtney James to the Affordable Housing Implementation Committee—after Charlie Reece sought and received clarification that ShotSpotter would only return if formally recommended by administration. Council then voted 6-0 (Jillian Johnson temporarily off the call) to settle the September 21 agenda before moving to closed session on the August 21 Rochelle Manor body-camera recordings.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager Priority Items
votes.discussion_detail: Jillian Johnson moved and Javiera Caballero seconded approving City Manager Tom Bonfield's priority items, including referring Item 10 back to administration and adding Duke Energy, Shannon Road culvert, and city manager search firm attachments. All seven members voted Aye.

votes.item_title: Approve City Attorney Priority Item for Closed Session (NCGS 143-318.11(a)(1))
votes.discussion_detail: Jillian Johnson moved and Charlie Reece seconded adding a closed session at the end of the meeting under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(1) and NCGS 132-1.4A to review law enforcement recordings from the August 21 Rochelle Manor incident. All seven members voted Aye.

votes.item_title: Settle Regular City Council Meeting Agenda
votes.notes: Mayor Schewel noted under COVID remote voting rules that an absent member does not count as an Aye.
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded settling the September 21 meeting agenda (Consent Items 1-5, 7-9, 11-14, 27; GBA Public Hearings 17-19, 26). Mayor Schewel announced the motion passed 6-0 with Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson absent from the vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept 10, 2020 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Proposed Six-Month Free Pilot of ShotSpotter Acoustic Gunshot Detection System
disagreements.summary: Council split sharply over whether to accept a no-cost six-month ShotSpotter pilot in three square miles of Durham, pitting members advocating immediate data and deterrence against daily neighborhood gunfire against members opposing increased armed police deployments and acoustic surveillance.
disagreements.side_a_position: Test ShotSpotter for six months at zero financial obligation to collect local data and address unreported gunfire traumatizing Black and Brown children.
side_a_arguments: Over 80% of gunfire goes unreported to 911 because residents feel resigned or fear retaliation, leaving children hiding in bathtubs and families traumatized.
A free, no-obligation six-month experiment lets Durham test accuracy and efficacy locally without committing funds, and root-cause alternatives have not yet received major budget funding.
disagreements.side_b_position: Decline ShotSpotter because independent evidence shows high false-positive rates and the system funnels more armed police officers and surveillance into communities of color rather than advancing non-police safety solutions.
side_b_arguments: Charlotte police officers reported confirming gunfire on only 1 in 41 ShotSpotter alerts, creating false-positive responses that strain police resources and heighten community tension.
Technology tied to cameras or drones expands surveillance and undermines Durham's shift toward unarmed crisis response, violence interrupters, and the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force.
disagreements.resolution: No council member offered a motion to proceed; Mayor Schewel closed the discussion at 03:58:43 and clarified at 05:16:37 that any future action would only occur if City Administration formally brought forward a recommendation.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept 10, 2020 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Local Minority-Owned Business Contracting vs. Intergovernmental Exemption in Texas A&M Transportation Institute (TTI) Transit Contract
disagreements.summary: During review of pulled Item 11 (a $100,000 intergovernmental contract with Texas A&M Transportation Institute), Council members debated whether to pause and restart procurement to include local Black- and minority-owned storytelling firms or proceed to meet urgent GoDurham transit funding deadlines.
disagreements.side_a_position: Consider restarting the procurement or splitting off the ~20% communications/storytelling scope so local minority-owned businesses can compete under an equity lens.
side_a_arguments: Intergovernmental contracts bypass Equal Business Opportunity Program compliance, and roughly $20,000 for visual storytelling could support qualified local Triangle firms.
Community advocates including the Transit Equity Campaign urged restarting the process to align with Durham's racial equity standards.
disagreements.side_b_position: Proceed with the TTI contract while adding GoDurham rider stakeholder language and TTI workforce demographics, because TTI's combined transit-data integration and communications skill set is urgently needed for County Transit Plan advocacy.
side_b_arguments: Restarting procurement or adding a subcontractor would significantly delay data needed to position GoDurham for Durham County Transit Plan funds.
Staff checked NC State and NCCU first without finding comparable transit-data integration capacity and committed to contracting with local M/WBE firms on larger upcoming transit projects.
disagreements.resolution: Staff agreed to revise Exhibit A to explicitly name GoDurham riders in communities of color and low-wealth neighborhoods as key stakeholders and attach TTI workforce demographic data ahead of the September 21 consent vote.

meetings.title: Special Durham City Council & DHA Meeting Sept 10, 2020 (with captions)
meetings.executive_summary: In the captioned recording of the September 10, 2020 joint virtual special meeting between the Durham City Council and the Durham Housing Authority (DHA) Board of Commissioners, leaders reviewed joint affordable housing investments, COVID-19 operations, and long-term public housing redevelopment. Community Development Director Reginald Johnson detailed City support including $1 million in emergency rental assistance through Durham County DSS, $700,000 for minor home repairs, $500,000 for eviction diversion with Legal Aid of NC, $1 million for East Durham redevelopment, $3 million in HUD lead remediation funds, and DDP relocation funding. DHA CEO Anthony Scott outlined McDougall Terrace environmental remediation, conversion of public housing units to HUD's Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD) voucher platform, and the 10-year, $500 million Downtown and Neighborhood Plan (DDP)—noting DHA won a 9% LIHTC award for Phase 1 of Liberty/519 East Main Street, removed former director Carvie S. Oldham Sr.'s name from 519 East Main due to his racist record, and remains committed to keeping low-income housing downtown.

agenda_items.title: Opening Remarks, DHA Board Introductions, and City-DHA Collaboration
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DHA Board Chair Dan introduced board members including long-serving commissioners George Quick and Laurie Nottingham and newly appointed Terrell Armstrong, emphasizing unprecedented cooperation with the City, County, DPS, Durham Tech, and nonprofits. Mayor Steve Schewel echoed appreciation for DHA CEO Anthony Scott and City staff in advancing affordable housing funded by the 2019 housing bond.

agenda_items.title: City Community Development Programs and COVID-19 Housing Relief
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented City programs partnering with DHA and community groups, highlighting nearly $2 million and $700,000 earmarked for DDP relocation, $1 million in COVID emergency rental assistance via DSS, $700,000 for minor home repair, $500,000 for eviction diversion, and a $3 million HUD lead remediation grant.

agenda_items.title: DHA Pandemic Response, RAD Conversions, Downtown Development Plan, and Anti-Displacement Commitment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DHA CEO Anthony Scott detailed COVID-19 safety protocols, RAD conversions (including Laurel Oaks and transferring 21 units to DHIC's Willard Street development), and the 17-phase, 10-year Downtown and Neighborhood Plan across seven sites (starting with J.J. Henderson renovations and 80 new senior units in spring 2021). Scott reported DHA's board removed the Oldham Towers name from 519 East Main Street over Carvie S. Oldham Sr.'s racist history, celebrated the Liberty/519 East Main Phase 1 9% tax credit award, and joined Mayor Schewel in affirming DHA will expand rather than sell off downtown affordable housing.

meetings.title: Virtual City Council Meeting Sept 8, 2020 (with captions)
meetings.executive_summary: In the captioned recording of the September 8, 2020 virtual regular meeting, the Durham City Council welcomed newly sworn-in Ward 3 Council Member Pierce Freelon and approved the Consent Agenda 7-0 after pulling Item 8 (Taser Replacement Program) due to public comments. On Item 13 (Trinity School Series 2020 tax-exempt revenue bond up to $6.75 million), Mark-Anthony Middleton criticized Council's prior denial of a charter school bond for Excelsior Classical Academy relative to approving a private Christian school lacking transportation, free lunch, or EC programs, before Council passed the TEFRA resolution 6-1 (Ayes: Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Pierce Freelon, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Charlie Reece; Nay: Javiera Caballero). Council continued public hearings on two southeastern Durham consolidated annexations—Leesville Road Assemblage to October 5 and 1101 Olive Branch Road to October 19—pending a September 24 infrastructure presentation, and referred Police Chief Cerelyn Davis's 250-Taser replacement contract back to administration after Jillian Johnson requested a work session on whether officers should continue carrying Tasers.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Welcome to Council Member Pierce Freelon, and City Manager Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order and welcomed Ward 3 Council Member Pierce Freelon, who pledged to honor Durham's elders and ancestors in his votes. City Manager Tom Bonfield presented updated attachments for Items 1 (Coronavirus Relief Fund plan), 8 (Taser replacement), and 9 (East Durham water and sewer rehabilitation).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval (Items 1-7 and 9, Pulling Item 8 Taser Replacement Program)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel pulled Item 8 (Taser Replacement Program) on behalf of roughly 20 written public commenters. DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded approving the remaining Consent Agenda items, which passed unanimously 7-0 on roll call.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Educational Facilities Revenue Bond (Trinity School Series 2020, Not to Exceed $6,750,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director David Boyd presented the federal TEFRA public hearing for up to $6.75 million in Public Finance Authority conduit bonds for Trinity School of Durham and Chapel Hill, carrying no city financial obligation. Following questioning by Mark-Anthony Middleton and Javiera Caballero and debate over Excelsior Classical Academy and vendor diversity, Council approved the resolution 6-1 with Javiera Caballero voting Nay.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Consolidated Annexation: Leesville Road Assemblage
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a public hearing on Tim Sivers and Horvath Associates' 107-acre Leesville Road Assemblage annexation and PDR 3.236 rezoning, discussing traffic impacts at Leesville Road, Olive Branch Road, and US 70 with Bill Judge. With the applicant's consent, Council continued the public hearing open to October 5 following the September 24 Searles infrastructure briefing.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Consolidated Annexation: 1101 Olive Branch Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented the 178-acre annexation and PDR 2.999 rezoning (up to 421 single-family and townhouse units) at 1101 Olive Branch Road, noting a 4-9 Planning Commission denial recommendation. Applicant attorney Jamie Schwedler requested a continuance until after the southeastern Durham briefing, and Council kept the hearing open until October 19.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item — Durham Police Department Taser Replacement Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Cerelyn Davis explained the request for 250 Tasers with a five-year maintenance and cartridge warranty to replace 212 inoperable units. After Jillian Johnson requested a work session to review Durham Beyond Policing's report and debate whether officers should carry Tasers—and Mark-Anthony Middleton, Charlie Reece, DeDreana Freeman, and Tom Bonfield weighed in on equipment safety and clarity of information requests—Mayor Schewel referred the item back to administration.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (Referred back to administration)

votes.item_title: Approve Consent Agenda (Items 1-7 and 9, Excluding Pulled Item 8)
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded approval of the Consent Agenda excluding pulled Item 8. All seven members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Item 13 — Adopt Resolution Approving Public Finance Authority Educational Facilities Revenue Bond (Trinity School Series 2020, Up to $6.75M)
votes.notes: Clerk corrected Mayor Schewel's initial unanimous announcement at 00:34:29 to record Javiera Caballero's Nay vote (6-1).

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual City Council Meeting Sept 8, 2020 (with captions)
disagreements.issue: Politicizing Pro Forma Conduit Bond Approvals vs. Consistent Racial Equity Standards in City Contracting (Trinity School TEFRA Bond)
disagreements.summary: Council debated consistency between denying Excelsior Classical Academy's charter bond and approving Trinity School's TEFRA conduit bond, as well as whether Council can reject city contracts based on vendor workforce demographics.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve Trinity School as a pro forma vote, while calling out inconsistency with the Excelsior denial and challenging Council to deny contracts to vendors lacking Black or Latino employees.
side_a_arguments: Neither bond created city financial exposure, yet Excelsior served low-income Black students with transportation, free lunch, and EC services while Trinity is a wealthy private school without them.
If equity standards are applied to pro forma votes, Council must apply them to companies seeking millions in city contracts.
disagreements.side_b_position: Charter schools now have a separate state DPI borrowing mechanism unlike private schools, and NC procurement law limits Council from rejecting goods/construction bids based on workforce data.
side_b_arguments: State law allows discretion on service contracts but restricts rejecting low-bid goods or building contracts over workforce statistics.
The City Attorney should provide a written legal memo clarifying Council's statutory limits.
disagreements.resolution: Council passed the Trinity School TEFRA resolution 6-1 (Javiera Caballero Nay) at 00:34:35, with staff and the City Attorney expected to report back on contracting discretion.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual City Council Meeting Sept 8, 2020 (with captions)
disagreements.issue: Police Department Taser Replacement Program vs. Work Session Review of Eliminating Tasers
disagreements.summary: Council split over whether to replace 212 inoperable police Tasers immediately or delay the contract for a work-session policy debate on removing Tasers from DPD's toolkit.
disagreements.side_a_position: Delay the purchase for a work session reviewing the Durham Beyond Policing memo and whether officers should carry Tasers.
side_a_arguments: Independent studies cited by Durham Beyond Policing argue Tasers fail to reduce overall use of force or improve safety.
Approving a five-year, 250-unit Taser contract requires deliberating whether that spending aligns with Council's public safety priorities.
disagreements.side_b_position: While Tasers remain authorized equipment, officers must not be left with 212 broken devices, and delayed policy objections should be clearly specified for staff research.
side_b_arguments: Officers deployed Tasers only 10 times in 2019 and rely on working less-lethal options in the field.
Council members requesting further research should send clear written questions to the City Manager and copy all colleagues.
disagreements.resolution: Mayor Schewel officially referred Item 8 back to administration at 02:21:19 without a vote.

meetings.title: Special Virtual Durham City Council Aug 31, 2020 (with captions)
meetings.executive_summary: Convening a brief virtual special meeting on August 31, 2020 to fill the vacant Ward 3 seat created by Representative Vernetta Alston's departure for the North Carolina General Assembly, all six seated members of the Durham City Council weighed remarks on five finalists (Sarah Sinning, Sheila Huggins, Leonardo Williams, Anita Daniels Keith, and Pierce Freelon). Charlie Reece, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, and Steve Schewel voiced support for Pierce Freelon—citing his deep Durham roots, artistic and youth mentorship, and commitment to racial equity and housing justice—while Mark-Anthony Middleton praised Anita Daniels Keith as combining the strengths of the entire field and DeDreana Freeman noted concerns over a predetermined feel while leaning toward Daniels Keith or Sheila Huggins. On the email ballot tally announced by the City Clerk, Council elected Pierce Freelon 4-2 over Anita Daniels Keith (Freelon: Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero; Daniels Keith: Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman), declining to convert the vote to unanimous and scheduling Freelon's socially distanced in-person swearing-in ahead of the September 8 meeting.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Remarks, and Appointment Vote for Vacant Ward 3 City Council Seat
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following brief technical delays reconnecting Charlie Reece, all six seated council members answered roll call and delivered statements on the five Ward 3 finalists before submitting email ballots to the City Clerk. The Clerk tallied 4 votes for Pierce Freelon (Charlie Reece, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Steve Schewel) and 2 votes for Anita Daniels Keith (Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman), electing Freelon to take office upon an in-person socially distanced swearing-in before September 8.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 4-2 (Email Ballot; Pierce Freelon 4, Anita Daniels Keith 2)

votes.item_title: Appointment to Vacant Ward 3 City Council Seat (Pierce Freelon vs. Anita Daniels Keith)
votes.notes: Because Pierce Freelon was the appointee being selected, only the six seated members voted. Here 'ayes' lists the 4 votes for Pierce Freelon and 'nays' lists the 2 votes for Anita Daniels Keith.
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted via email ballots submitted to the City Clerk after individual remarks: Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, and Javiera Caballero voted for Pierce Freelon, while Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman voted for Anita Daniels Keith. Mayor Schewel asked whether there was interest in making the selection unanimous, which did not happen, leaving the official tally at 4-2.

disagreements.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council Aug 31, 2020 (with captions)
disagreements.issue: Ward 3 City Council Vacancy Selection (Pierce Freelon vs. Anita Daniels Keith)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 4-2 in selecting Vernetta Alston's successor for Ward 3, with four members backing Pierce Freelon's vision and advocacy and two supporting Anita Daniels Keith amid concerns about process transparency and perceived predetermination.
disagreements.side_a_position: Appoint Pierce Freelon to fill the Ward 3 vacancy.
side_a_arguments: Freelon brings deep Ward 3 roots, youth mentorship, arts leadership, and clear alignment on racial equity, police reform, and housing justice.
His hopeful, unapologetic advocacy and past citywide campaign experience equip him to serve effectively until voters decide in the next election.
disagreements.side_b_position: Support Anita Daniels Keith as a custodial steward of the seat and raise concern that the outcome felt predetermined.
side_b_arguments: Daniels Keith's temperament, mental health/social service leadership, and community rootedness best represent a custodial stewardship role until voters weigh in.
Community correspondence (including from the Durham Committee) raised concerns that the appointment felt predetermined toward Freelon despite strong alternative finalists.
disagreements.resolution: Pierce Freelon was elected 4-2 on the first ballot at 00:27:54; Council declined to make the vote unanimous, though Javiera Caballero urged all members to welcome and support Freelon as a colleague.

meetings.title: Special Virtual Durham City Council August 27, 2020 (w/ captions)
meetings.executive_summary: In this captioned broadcast of the August 27, 2020 special virtual meeting, all six seated members of the Durham City Council interviewed the five finalists for the Ward 3 City Council vacancy, beginning with opening remarks and questioning of Anita Daniels-Kenney on housing wealth grants, decriminalizing drug paraphernalia in favor of mental-health treatment, and Northeast Central Durham community engagement. Following the interviews, Council took up an emergency $338,000 request from the City's $5 million COVID Relief Fund to extend community learning centers—including downtown capacity at Kates Corner and six school-affiliated sites—for 338 students from six weeks to 11 weeks. Council voted unanimously 6-0 on a roll-call motion by Charlie Reece, seconded by Jillian Johnson, to suspend the rules, and then passed the $338,000 allocation 5-1 on a motion by Mark-Anthony Middleton, seconded by Jillian Johnson, with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting Nay over transparency, late agenda placement, and county school-funding obligations.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Simultaneous Spanish Interpretation, and Interview Rules
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the special meeting to interview the five Ward 3 vacancy finalists, working with Council Member Javiera Caballero, the City Clerk, and Spanish interpreter Muadado to configure Zoom's simultaneous Spanish interpretation channel. Mayor Schewel explained that each candidate would receive a three-minute opening statement, up to eight minutes of questions per council member in rotating alphabetical order, and five minutes from the Mayor.

agenda_items.title: Interviews of Ward 3 Vacancy Finalists (Including Anita Daniels-Kenney)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: First finalist Anita Daniels-Kenney shared her personal background in public housing and answered Javiera Caballero's questions on fiscal priorities following the city's $8.7 million fund balance draw (proposing grants to help three to five families purchase homes) and on reforming low-level drug paraphernalia charges by treating addiction as a mental illness. DeDreana Freeman then began questioning Daniels-Kenney on engaging previously unengaged residents, citing her Triangle United Way work in Northeast Central Durham, before the remaining interviews continued through the middle of the meeting.

agenda_items.title: COVID Relief Fund Request of $338,000 for Community Learning Centers
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Presenters Mr. Perry, Ms. Gonzalez Smith, and Mrs. Zagbaya requested $338,000 from the City's COVID Relief Fund to bridge Durham County's six-week commitment up to 11 weeks for 338 students across six schools and partner sites such as Kates Corner downtown (~80 seats), while noting $202,000 as a nine-week alternative figure and confirming DPS had not guaranteed transportation. Deputy City Attorney Don O'Toole noted he could not immediately answer legal scope questions in City Attorney Rehberg's absence, and council members criticized the nearly 55-45 city-county split, the lack of work-session agenda notice, and the need for Durham County and DPS to shoulder ongoing funding. After a 6-0 roll-call suspension of the rules, Council approved the $338,000 expenditure 5-1 with DeDreana Freeman dissenting.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 5-1 (Roll Call; preceded by 6-0 rule suspension)

votes.item_title: Motion to Suspend the Rules for Action on $338,000 Community Learning Centers Request
votes.discussion_detail: After Charlie Reece raised a point of order requiring a rule suspension to vote on the special-meeting item, Reece moved and Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson seconded suspending the rules. All six seated council members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Approve $338,000 Expenditure from COVID Relief Fund for Community Learning Centers
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson seconded approving $338,000 from the COVID Relief Fund for community learning centers. During pre-vote discussion, DeDreana Freeman stated she supported the centers in principle but could not vote yes given the two-day emergency timeline and lack of public agenda transparency; the roll-call vote passed 5-1 with Freeman voting Nay.

disagreements.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council August 27, 2020 (w/ captions)
disagreements.issue: Transparency, Agenda Notice, and County Responsibility for $338,000 Learning Centers Funding
disagreements.summary: Council split 5-1 on approving $338,000 from the City's $5 million COVID Relief Fund for community learning centers, contrasting urgent pandemic student need against lack of work-session agenda transparency and Durham County's primary statutory role in funding public education.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve $338,000 in emergency COVID Relief funds immediately to launch 11 weeks of learning center seats by September 8 while emphasizing future funding must come from Durham County, DPS, and private donors.
side_a_arguments: Providing 11 weeks of learning center support for 338 students addresses an acute pandemic need before the September 8 start date.
The DPS Foundation is actively fundraising for the second semester, and partial immediate support is better than leaving students unserved.
disagreements.side_b_position: Withhold support because the funding request bypassed normal work-session public agenda notice and disproportionately taps the City's limited $5 million COVID Relief Fund.
side_b_arguments: The original ask and supporting documents never appeared on the work session agenda and were only placed on a late special-meeting agenda.
Durham County received far greater federal CARES funding and carries legal responsibility for funding Durham Public Schools.
disagreements.resolution: Motion passed 5-1 on roll call (Schewel, Johnson, Caballero, Middleton, Reece Aye; Freeman Nay).

meetings.title: Special Virtual Durham City Council August 24, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting virtually on August 24, 2020 with all six seated members present, the Durham City Council convened to select finalists from 12 applicants for the Ward 3 council vacancy. On a 6-0 roll-call motion by Charlie Reece, seconded by DeDreana Freeman, Council voted to accept Micah Furlong's application as timely after Furlong registered to vote on August 21 upon learning of the registration gap. Following an electronic ballot tallied by the City Clerk, Council voted unanimously 6-0 on a motion by Charlie Reece, seconded by Javiera Caballero, to advance the five candidates who received at least four votes—Anita Daniels-Kenney, Leonardo Q. Williams, Pierce Freelon, Sheila Ann Huggins (five votes each), and Sarah Sinning (four votes). Council then resolved differences over interview length, PowerPoints, finalist count, and advance question sharing by agreeing to three-minute spoken opening statements, up to eight minutes of questioning per council member with optional advance question sharing, and rotating first questioners alphabetically on August 27.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Roll Call Following Zoom Outage
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel waited for colleagues experiencing nationwide Zoom login problems and thanked the Clerk's Office and Technology Solutions for resolving access. The City Clerk called the roll at 00:02:01, confirming all six seated members were present.

agenda_items.title: Consideration of Micah Furlong's Ward 3 Application
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel explained that all 12 applicants who submitted by 5:00 p.m. on August 20 passed county tax verification, but Micah Furlong was not yet registered to vote at the time of checking and went to the Board of Elections on August 21 to register. Charlie Reece recommended considering Furlong's application based on good-faith effort and prompt correction, and Council approved his motion 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Electronic Ballot and Selection of Five Ward 3 Finalists
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After DeDreana Freeman resolved an Outlook form permission issue and all six members submitted electronic ballots, the City Clerk reported four applicants received five votes and one received four votes. Council voted unanimously 6-0 to advance the five finalists—Anita Daniels-Kenney, Leonardo Q. Williams, Pierce Freelon, Sheila Ann Huggins, and Sarah Sinning.

agenda_items.title: August 27 Finalist Interview Structure, Time Limits, and Question Sharing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated whether to keep eight-minute questioning rounds or reduce them to five minutes, whether to permit PowerPoint slides or narrow the pool to four finalists, and whether to share questions beforehand. Council agreed to schedule 50-minute slots starting at 5:00 p.m. on August 27 with three-minute spoken opening statements (no PowerPoints), up to eight minutes per council member (five minutes for the Mayor last), alphabetical rotation of the lead questioner, and optional advance question sharing.

votes.item_title: Consider Ward 3 Applicant Micah Furlong's Application Alongside Other Applications
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded allowing Micah Furlong's application to be considered despite registering to vote on August 21 after the August 20 filing deadline. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Advance Five Finalists Receiving at Least Four Votes for Ward 3 Vacancy Interviews
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and Javiera Caballero seconded advancing the five candidates who received at least four votes on the electronic ballot (Anita Daniels-Kenney, Leonardo Q. Williams, Pierce Freelon, Sheila Ann Huggins, and Sarah Sinning). The clerk called the roll and all six members voted Aye.

disagreements.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council August 24, 2020 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Structure of Ward 3 Finalist Interviews (Time Limits, Advance Questions, and Finalist Count)
disagreements.summary: Council members held differing views on shortening questioning rounds from eight to five minutes, requiring or encouraging advance submission of questions, permitting PowerPoint slides, and whether to interview four instead of five finalists.
disagreements.side_a_position: Favor shorter five-minute rounds, advance question sharing with candidates and colleagues, or reducing to four finalists to keep the August 27 interview meeting concise.
side_a_arguments: Five 50-minute Zoom interviews create an exhausting four-hour session.
Sharing questions ahead of time avoids duplicate questioning and helps candidates prepare concise responses.
Limiting the pool to four finalists could also shorten the meeting if time is a major concern.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain the established eight-minute questioning cap and preserve unscripted live questioning (or require PowerPoints if time is cut).
side_b_arguments: Council is a deliberative body that needs to see candidates think and engage on their feet rather than read scripted answers.
Individual members can already govern themselves and use fewer than eight minutes without lowering the formal cap.
Cutting questioning to five minutes without a PowerPoint option could limit the information gathered from candidates.
disagreements.resolution: Council maintained five finalists, kept the eight-minute cap (with Charlie Reece voluntarily taking five minutes), allowed optional advance sharing of questions and candidate materials, and prohibited PowerPoints in three-minute openings.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session August 20, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting virtually on August 20, 2020 after a 2.5-hour closed-session evaluation of the City Clerk and City Attorney, five seated members of the Durham City Council voted 5-0 (with DeDreana Freeman absent due to initial technical difficulties) to approve the City Manager's priority items on a motion by Jillian Johnson, seconded by Charlie Reece. During work-session reviews, Transportation Director Sean Egan confirmed coordination with Council Member Freeman's racial equity initiative on parking fines and fees, Police staff addressed Taser replacement costs and vendor workforce diversity, and Budget Director Bertha Johnson presented the $2.9 million CARES Act Coronavirus Relief Fund plan, noting a $234,000 adjustment on the Health Ambassadors program and constraints on delinquent water bill aid. Police Chief C.J. Davis then delivered the 2020 Second Quarter Crime Report covering staffing vacancies, 1,300+ light-duty call responses, George Floyd protest responses, five reported hate crimes, and community outreach. After discussing county-city coordination on the Property Tax Relief Program, all six members voted unanimously 6-0 on a motion by Charlie Reece, seconded by Javiera Caballero, to settle the upcoming regular agenda.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and City Manager's Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the 1:00 p.m. work session to order following a closed-session annual evaluation of the City Clerk and City Attorney, with DeDreana Freeman delayed by technical difficulties. The acting City Manager presented attachment updates for Item 2 (2021 City Council meeting schedule), Item 12 (2020 Q2 Crime Report), and Item 16 (Property Tax Relief Program), which Council approved 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Departmental Agenda Review, Parking Penalties Equity, and Taser Replacement Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Items 1, 2, 3, and 8 for discussion and requested email follow-up on Item 6 (Town of Hillsborough mutual aid water supply history). On Item 3, Transportation Director Sean Egan confirmed his department is supplying data to Council Member DeDreana Freeman's fines-and-fees racial equity effort; on Item 8, council members questioned vendor workforce diversity and Taser deployment frequency, with police staff explaining Tasers are rarely deployed and a five-year replacement plan (~$1,500 per unit) reduces ad-hoc repair costs.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Durham City Coronavirus Relief Fund (CRF) Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson presented the $2.9 million CARES Act Coronavirus Relief Fund allocation plan due to Durham County by August 28. She reported that after County General Manager Jodi Miller identified ineligible Health Ambassadors costs, the City's 50% share dropped to $89,000 (saving $234,000 contingent on County approval), and explained delinquent water bills were excluded due to strict COVID-19 hardship verification rules and unknown totals until late September.

agenda_items.title: Durham Police Department 2020 Second Quarter Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief C.J. Davis and police leadership presented Q2 2020 metrics, noting light-duty officers handled 1,300+ service calls, sworn staffing stood at 93% (with ~30 vacancies pending fall BLET) and non-sworn at 89%, 48 U-visas were processed (58% approved), and four resignations occurred in lieu of Internal Affairs investigations alongside retirements and separations. Chief Davis also discussed malware recovery, facilitating peaceful George Floyd protests and a June 22 unity march with Sheriff Birkhead, five reported hate crimes (two anti-white, three anti-black), and community outreach; Council discussed clearance rates, response times, and therapy needs for gun-violence victims.

agenda_items.title: Property Tax Relief Program Follow-Up, Settling Regular Agenda, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Charlie Reece noted staff guidance is needed on official city action to join Durham County's Property Tax Relief Program for the city portion of property tax bills, while leaving Item 16 informational for now. Council unanimously voted 6-0 to settle Consent Items 1-9 and General Business public hearings 13-15, and DeDreana Freeman (having joined after earlier technical trouble) highlighted Mark-Anthony Middleton's recorded universal basic income presentation with End Poverty Durham.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager's Priority Items (Updates to Items 2, 12, and 16)
votes.notes: Freeman later confirmed at 03:30:09 that technical difficulties prevented her from joining at the start of the meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson moved and Charlie Reece seconded approving the acting City Manager's priority items updating attachments for Items 2, 12, and 16. Five members voted Aye on roll call; DeDreana Freeman was not yet connected due to technical difficulties.

votes.item_title: Settle Regular Meeting Agenda (Consent Items 1-9; GBA Public Hearings Items 13-15)
votes.discussion_detail: Following confirmation that Item 16 remained informational, Charlie Reece moved and Javiera Caballero seconded settling the upcoming regular agenda with Consent Items 1-9 and General Business Public Hearings Items 13-15. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council August 17, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Convening virtually on August 17, 2020 with all six seated members present, the Durham City Council approved the Consent Agenda unanimously 6-0 on a motion by Charlie Reece, seconded by DeDreana Freeman, authorizing a PolicyLink Fines and Fees Justice grant, an FAA RDU Airport grant, eight replacement GoDurham buses for service expansion, a Triangle Land Conservancy Down to Earth Farms watershed agreement, the Discover Durham 'Back on the Bull' campaign, and a $600,000 COVID-19 Public Health Ambassador Initiative shared with Durham County and UNC Gillings School of Public Health. Council then held a public hearing on Item 11 (Cases A1900008 / Z1900023, Farrington Towns), questioning Planning staff Emily Ann Brothers and applicant Jared Edens about why the Planning Commission shifted from an 11-1 approval recommendation in December to a 6-7 failure in June after removal of a wetland retention commitment. Confirming that aerials showed wooded wetland requiring USACE/NCDEQ permitting if filled rather than an unbuffered pond, Council approved the Future Land Use Map amendment, consistency statement, and UDO zoning ordinance across three unanimous 6-0 roll-call votes, before discussing the September restoration of public consent-agenda pulls and work-session public comment.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Pledge of Allegiance, Roll Call, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the 7:00 p.m. meeting to order, led a moment of silent meditation, Charlie Reece led the Pledge of Allegiance, and all six seated members answered roll call. Mark-Anthony Middleton expressed sympathy for families affected by recent gunfire, a colleague praised DPS educators launching remote learning for 33,000 students, and DeDreana Freeman noted upcoming 100th-anniversary celebrations of women's suffrage.

agenda_items.title: Manager's Priority Updates and Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager noted added info on Item 8 (Down to Earth Farms watershed protection) and placed supplemental Items 13 (Discover Durham 'Back on the Bull' campaign) and 14 (interlocal agreements with Durham County and UNC Gillings School of Public Health for the COVID-19 Public Health Ambassador Initiative) onto Consent without objection. Council clarified Items 13 and 14 totaled $600,000 (not duplicated) with 50% County reimbursement, thanked staff including Aaron Paris on the PolicyLink Fines and Fees Justice grant (Item 3), highlighted eight replacement GoDurham buses (Item 7), and passed the Consent Agenda 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Farrington Towns Annexation / FLUM & Rezoning (A1900008 / Z1900023)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Emily Ann Brothers presented the Future Land Use Map amendment (Low Density to Low-Medium Density Residential, maintaining the Falls/Jordan watershed overlay) and zoning map change for Farrington Towns, noting the Planning Commission voted 11-1 in December but failed 6-7 in June after the applicant removed a wetland retention proffer. Following questions from Charlie Reece, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and DeDreana Freeman to staff and applicant Jared Edens confirming stormwater review at site plan and federal/state wetland permitting, Council adopted the FLUM amendment, consistency statement, and UDO zoning ordinance in three 6-0 roll-call votes.

agenda_items.title: Restoration of Public Consent Agenda Pulls and Work Session Public Comment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel and Council Member Charlie Reece discussed restoring residents' ability to pull items from the consent agenda at Monday regular meetings beginning September 8, as well as restoring public comment during work sessions by the end of September.

votes.item_title: Item 11 (Z1900023 Farrington Towns) — Adopt Resolution Amending Future Land Use Map to Low-Medium Density Residential
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting the resolution amending the Future Land Use Map for Farrington Towns from Low Density to Low-Medium Density Residential. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Item 11 (Z1900023 Farrington Towns) — Adopt Consistency Statement
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the consistency statement for Z1900023. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Item 11 (Z1900023 Farrington Towns) — Adopt Ordinance Amending the UDO
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson moved and Charlie Reece seconded (with Mark-Anthony Middleton also seconding/thirding) adopting the ordinance amending the UDO zoning map for Farrington Towns. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session August 6, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At its August 6, 2020 virtual work session with all six seated members present, the Durham City Council opened with constituent updates from Charlie Reece and Mark-Anthony Middleton regarding a Rewood Estates neighborhood development near NC 55 and a 75th-anniversary sister-city celebration with Toyama, Japan, before unanimously voting 6-0 to approve the City Manager's priority items (including a rule-suspension request on a time-sensitive NACTO pandemic streets grant and a closed session on personnel matters). Following review of consent items—including the PolicyLink Fines and Fees Justice grant, eight GoDurham replacement buses, and the Down to Earth Farms watershed project—Council deliberated extensively on supplemental Item 12 establishing the Ward 3 vacancy appointment process. Members resolved questions over whether to fix finalist numbers before applications closed on August 20 by unanimously voting 6-0 on a motion by DeDreana Freeman, seconded by Charlie Reece, to advance three to seven finalists and schedule special selection meetings on August 24 and August 31. Council then voted 6-0 to settle the regular agenda and 6-0 to enter closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) regarding conditions of appointing an interim city manager and an employee complaint investigation.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Neighborhood Concerns, and Sister-City Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the 1:00 p.m. work session to order and all six seated members answered roll call. Charlie Reece (joined by Mark-Anthony Middleton) briefed colleagues on a nearly two-hour call with Rewood Estates residents about an adjacent development near NC 55 and celebrated the 75th-anniversary virtual event with sister city Toyama, Japan, while members also praised staff flexibility for working parents and noted a vendor offer for a no-cost six-month technology pilot.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items (Minutes, NACTO Grant, Ward 3 Vacancy, Closed Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager committed to scheduling Middleton's requested items and providing a memo on DPR/Office on Youth after-school and childcare support, then presented priority items: minutes updates (Item 1), a request to suspend rules for same-day action on a NACTO Streets for Pandemic Response and Recovery grant due to an October 1 start and November 1 expenditure deadline (Item 6), supplemental Ward 3 vacancy timeline discussion (Item 12), and a closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6). Council approved the priority items 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Administrative Consent Items Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel reviewed administrative consent items including the PolicyLink Fines and Fees Justice grant (Item 3, crediting DeDreana Freeman), the Joint City-County Renewal and Recovery Task Force recommendations presentation (Item 4), an RDU FAA Airport Improvement grant (Item 5), eight GoDurham replacement buses for service expansion (Item 7), and the Down to Earth Farms watershed project (Item 8, with a question on whether the $424,000 landowner contribution was a land donation).

agenda_items.title: Ward 3 Vacancy Appointment Timeline and Finalist Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated how many Ward 3 vacancy finalists to select given that applications would remain open until August 20 at 5:00 p.m., weighing Charlie Reece's caution against locking in a number before knowing applicant volume against DeDreana Freeman's and Jillian Johnson's suggestions for a minimum-maximum range. Council scheduled special meetings at 10:15 a.m. on August 24 and August 31 and voted 6-0 to advance between three and seven qualified finalists.

agenda_items.title: Settling the Regular Agenda and Entering Closed Session on Personnel Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following the City Manager's recommendation grouping Consent Items 1-3, 5, 7-10, updated Item 12, two Recovery & Renewal Task Force items (13 and 14), and GBA Public Hearing Item 11, Council voted 6-0 to settle the agenda. DeDreana Freeman then read and moved a motion under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) to enter closed session on interim city manager appointment conditions and an individual employee complaint investigation, which passed 6-0.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager's Priority Items (Items 1, 6, 12, and Closed Session Request)
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson moved and Charlie Reece seconded approving the City Manager's priority items. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Approve Ward 3 Vacancy Selection Process (Advancing Three to Seven Finalists)
votes.discussion_detail: After Mayor Schewel summarized the Ward 3 appointment process moving forward with between three and seven qualified finalists and special meetings on August 24 and August 31, DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded the process. Mayor Schewel, Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, and Mark-Anthony Middleton voted Aye on roll call (with Caballero having voiced support for Reece's timeline earlier and Reece's final response falling at the end-of-roll gap).

votes.item_title: Settle Regular Meeting Agenda (Consent Items 1-3, 5, 7-10, 12, 13-14; GBA Item 11)
votes.notes: Mover was not explicitly identified by name in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the City Manager's recommendation on Consent and GBA public hearing items, a council member moved and Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson seconded settling the agenda. All six members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Enter Closed Session Pursuant to NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) (Interim City Manager Conditions & Employee Complaint)
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded going into closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) to consider conditions of appointment of an interim city manager and an investigation of a complaint against an individual employee. All six members voted Aye on roll call.
