agenda_items.title: Clerk Priority Item Addition and Administrative Consent Agenda Pulls
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 6-0 to add City Clerk Diana Schreiber's priority item on reactivating boards and commissions to the end of the work session. Mayor Schewel noted minor corrections to the March 5 minutes and members pulled Items 10, 17, 18, 19, and 20 for discussion ahead of the May 4 regular meeting.

agenda_items.title: Item 10: Contract with Housing for New Hope as Unsheltered Coordinating Agency
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff (Karen Lado and Hanaleah Hoberman) answered questions from Mayor Schewel and Mayor Pro Tem Johnson regarding COVID-19 training for street outreach workers, medical partnerships with Duke Clinic and Lincoln Community Health, moving medically vulnerable unsheltered residents into hotels, and Housing for New Hope's expansion to five dedicated program staff.

agenda_items.title: Items 17 & 18: Police District 1 Substation Lease and 1415 W. Club Blvd. Property Sale
agenda_items.discussion_summary: On Item 17 (10-year, $2.9 million Police District 1 substation lease at 915 Holloway St.), Council Member Freeman questioned General Services staff (David Fleischer) on the absence of Office of Equity and Inclusion review for city leases. On Item 18 (sale of a 30x36-foot residual parcel at 1415 W. Club Blvd.), Freeman asked about affordability conditions while Mayor Pro Tem Johnson proposed directing proceeds into the Dedicated Housing Fund and creating a standing policy for future residential land sales.

agenda_items.title: Items 19 & 20: Recycling Processing Contract and Durham County Transit Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Solid Waste staff reported recycling costs swung from $450,000 revenue to over $100/ton (versus ~$40/ton landfilling), while continuing single-stream collection with public education and regional Triangle J coordination. Transportation Director Sean Egan and MPO representative Aaron Cain reviewed the $670,000 Durham County Transit Plan consultant contract and addressed questions from Mayor Schewel and Council Member Freeman about GoDurham's 16-passenger social-distancing cap leaving riders at stops and plans to deploy follow-on buses.

agenda_items.title: Virtual Operations Guidelines for Boards, Committees, and Commissions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated how to allow eager advisory boards to resume work virtually without disadvantaging members lacking internet access, childcare bandwidth, or time during the pandemic, with Reece and Freeman urging caution and Middleton supporting authorizing but not mandating meetings. Council tasked Mayor Pro Tem Johnson and Council Member Caballero with drafting voluntary, no-penalty guidelines using Zoom or Microsoft Teams with tech liaisons and telephone dial-in options.

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Nominations and Settling May 4 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Because six seated members required four votes for nomination, council broke ties via announced vote switches for the Citizens Advisory Committee (Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman), BPAC (Shyla Nappe and Jasmine Joyner), Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee (Cesar Angiano-Ortiz and Shan Almonte), and Recreation Advisory Commission (Cedric Burke), and confirmed Appearance, DPAC Oversight, and Workers Rights nominees. City Manager Bonfield then recommended placing Items 1–4, 6–13, and 17–20 on the May 4 consent agenda, which council approved 6-0.

votes.notes: Vote taken by hand raise on Zoom; mover not named on audio.
votes.discussion_detail: Added the City Clerk's priority item regarding virtual operation of boards and commissions to the end of the work session agenda.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council April 20, 2020 (with closed captions)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the April 20, 2020 virtual City Council meeting with all six seated members present following Vernetta Alston's resignation. Council announced an expansion of written public comments from 250 to 4,000 characters, approved the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 8) 6-0, and approved Item 8 (Emergency Response Plan and Source Water Risk and Resilience Plan) 6-0. Turning to the Ward 3 vacancy after community groups criticized the April 6 appointment timeline during the pandemic, council accepted legal guidance from City Attorney Kim Rehberg and voted unanimously 6-0 to rescind the April 6 timeline and unanimously 6-0 to proceed instead under N.C.G.S. § 160A-63 (via § 160A-3), removing the charter's 60-day special-election clock and targeting an August 6 check-in.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, COVID-19 Update, and Public Comment Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order with a moment of silence for 86 COVID-19 residents at a Durham rehabilitation facility and community deaths, followed by the Pledge and roll call. Schewel noted public comments on North Durham motorbikes and rent hardship, confirmed the public comment limit increased to 4,000 characters, and reviewed Duke health modeling showing slower case growth.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1–3, 5–7, 9–23, Excluding Item 8)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved all consent items except pulled Item 8, encompassing CDBG contracts with Urban Ministries and DHA for Laurel Oaks Townhomes, DHA's McDougall Terrace grant request, Eno River water-supply reclassification support, sewer manhole rehabilitation contracts, the Museum of Durham History lease, Hoover Road Park CMAR amendment, 2019 Q4 crime report, and the Ashton Place Development Loan commitment.

agenda_items.title: Item 8: Emergency Response Plan and Source Water Risk and Resilience Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman stated she pulled Item 8 to highlight appreciation for staff's quick response, after which council passed the item unanimously by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Rescission of April 6 Ward 3 Timeline and Election to Proceed Under N.C.G.S. § 160A-63
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton urged rescinding the April 6 appointment schedule due to pandemic access barriers raised by the Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People, People's Alliance, and Friends of Durham. After Council Member Charlie Reece and City Attorney Kim Rehberg outlined how N.C.G.S. § 160A-3 and § 160A-63 eliminate the charter's 60-day deadline while preserving appointment authority, council agreed to revisit the process on August 6 and passed both the rescission (6-0) and § 160A-63 election (6-0).

votes.notes: Mover and seconder not named on audio.
votes.discussion_detail: Passed unanimously by voice vote following brief supportive remarks by Council Member Freeman.

votes.item_title: Elect to Fill Ward 3 Vacancy Under N.C.G.S. § 160A-63
votes.notes: Transcribed in ASR as '168-63'; council targeted August 6 for follow-up review.
votes.discussion_detail: Elected under N.C.G.S. § 160A-3 to fill the Ward 3 vacancy pursuant to N.C.G.S. § 160A-63 without the 60-day charter clock.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Virtual Work Session April 9, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over Durham City Council's first virtual work session on April 9, 2020, with all seven seated members present—marking Council Member Vernetta Alston's final meeting before her resignation took effect at midnight to join the North Carolina General Assembly. Council voted 7-0 to approve priority agenda additions (referring Item 4 Forest Hills Neighborhood Protection Overlay back to staff and adding supplemental Item 23 Ashton Place Development Loan Commitment), reviewed pulled consent items (including the Museum of Durham History lease, Hoover Road Park CMAR contract, VCISO cybersecurity services after the malware attack, and the Ashton Place tax-credit loan), and clarified minutes procedures. Council also voted unanimously 7-0 to authorize the City Manager to receive and expend a private foundation donation for emergent COVID-19 child-feeding and homelessness needs, and voted 7-0 to settle the April 20 regular agenda.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Farewell Tributes to Vernetta Alston, and Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel opened the council's first virtual work session, and council members offered farewell tributes to Ward 3 Council Member Vernetta Alston ahead of her midnight resignation. Council voted 7-0 to approve priority items presented by City Manager Tom Bonfield—referring Item 4 (Forest Hills NPO) back to administration, updating Item 17 (2019 Q4 Crime Report), adding supplemental Item 23 (Ashton Place Development Loan Commitment), and adding the Mayor's COVID-19 private donation item.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review and Pulled Items (Items 1, 14, 15, 21, 22, 23)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed backlog items from March 5 and new items including McDougall Terrace grant funding (Item 7) and pulled Items 1, 14, 15, 21, 22, and 23. Discussions covered Clerk minutes-summarization rules versus 'for the record' requests (Item 1), the 15-year Museum of Durham History lease with a 10-year clawback (Item 14), the Hoover Road Park soccer complex CMAR amendment (Item 15), VCISO cybersecurity recovery following the city's malware event (Item 22), and the Ashton Place affordable housing tax-credit loan commitment (Item 23).

agenda_items.title: Authorization to Accept and Expend Private Foundation COVID-19 Donation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel reported that a local private foundation sought to donate emergency funds to the city for immediate COVID-19 needs such as feeding students and seniors and homelessness support. Council members urged prioritizing rent/eviction relief for undocumented and vulnerable households alongside the countywide feeding plan, and voted 7-0 to authorize the City Manager to expend up to the amount received and report back to council.

agenda_items.title: Settle April 20 Agenda and Discuss Virtual Public Comment, Hearings, and Closed Sessions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 7-0 to settle the April 20 regular agenda (all items on consent) after noting the efficiency of reviewing 23 items virtually in about an hour. City Manager Bonfield noted budget staff would schedule an April budget session, and City Attorney Kim Rehberg advised updating council individually on a mediated legal case rather than holding a virtual closed session.

votes.item_title: City Manager and Mayor Priority Items (Items 4, 17, 23, and COVID-19 Donation Item)
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote; mover not named on audio.
votes.discussion_detail: Referred Item 4 (Forest Hills NPO) back to administration, acknowledged Item 17 attachments, and added Item 23 (Ashton Place loan commitment) and the COVID-19 foundation donation item.

votes.item_title: Authorize City Manager to Receive and Expend Private Foundation COVID-19 Donation
votes.notes: Council Member Middleton requested adding 'not to exceed the amount received from the donor'; passed unanimously by voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Authorized the City Manager, upon receipt of the private donation within 10 days for emergent COVID-19 needs (feeding and homelessness), to spend up to the amount received and report back to council.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Virtual Meeting April 6, 2020 (with closed captions)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over Durham City Council's first full virtual meeting on April 6, 2020, with all seven seated members participating. The session featured COVID-19 operational briefings from the Emergency Operations Center, GoDurham transit, Police Chief C.J. Davis on non-punitive Stay-at-Home enforcement, homelessness shelter-to-hotel relocation (Colin Davis), small business recovery via DurhamBusiness360.com (Andre Pettigrew), and projected FY 2020-21 revenue shortfalls (Bertha Johnson). Council voted 7-0 by roll call to reluctantly accept Council Member Vernetta Alston's resignation effective April 9. On a 5-2 split roll-call vote, Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Vernetta Alston, and Javiera Caballero voted Aye to adopt a 30-day Ward 3 appointment schedule (April 13–May 4), while DeDreana Freeman and Mark-Anthony Middleton voted Nay due to pandemic equity and access concerns.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Proclamations, and COVID-19 Departmental & EOC Briefings
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel opened the virtual meeting, read proclamations for National Community Development Week and National Crime Victims' Rights Week, and led COVID-19 response briefings. Briefings covered 700 teleworking staff and 911 malware recovery, transit safety and restaurant pickup zones, Chief Davis's non-punitive Stay-at-Home enforcement and mask policy, and EOC work to relocate medically vulnerable shelter residents into hotels pending county contract action.

agenda_items.title: COVID-19 Small Business Support and Revised Budget Outlook
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD Director Andre Pettigrew outlined small business webinars and the new DurhamBusiness360.com portal alongside NCWorks unemployment processing delays. Budget Director Bertha Johnson reported projected 10% sales tax losses on Durham's ~$71M baseline and up to 20% discretionary revenue declines, noting budget guidelines would be revised before May 18.

agenda_items.title: Acceptance of Vernetta Alston's Resignation and Ward 3 Vacancy Replacement Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Charlie Reece presented an adjusted 30-day Ward 3 appointment timeline (posting April 13, applications due April 23, finalists April 27, interviews April 30, appointment May 4). Council Member Middleton advocated deferring to a special election given pandemic barriers and a Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People resolution, and Freeman opposed rushing a 30-day process; council voted 7-0 to accept Alston's resignation and 5-2 to approve the 30-day schedule.

votes.item_title: Accept Resignation of Council Member Vernetta Alston (Effective April 9, 2020)
votes.notes: Roll call vote; all 7 members voted Aye.
votes.discussion_detail: Reluctantly accepted Council Member Vernetta Alston's resignation effective April 9, 2020 at 11:59 p.m.

votes.item_title: Adopt 30-Day Schedule to Appoint Ward 3 Council Successor
votes.notes: Roll call vote: Schewel, Johnson, Reece, Alston, Caballero Aye; Freeman, Middleton Nay.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved the April 13–May 4 schedule for Ward 3 appointment applications, finalist selection, virtual interviews, and vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Virtual Meeting April 6, 2020 (with closed captions)
disagreements.issue: Ward 3 Vacancy Process: 30-Day Charter Appointment Schedule vs. Deferral / Special Election During COVID-19
disagreements.summary: Council split 5-2 over whether to conduct an accelerated 30-day virtual appointment process under the City Charter or defer the Ward 3 seat to a special election because of COVID-19 access barriers.
disagreements.side_a_position: Proceed with an April 13–May 4 appointment schedule to comply with the City Charter's 'shall' mandate, seat a seventh member before the June budget vote, and avoid special-election costs.
side_a_arguments: City Charter mandates an appointment attempt within 60 days unless council deadlocks.
A May 4 appointment avoids an eight-month Ward 3 vacancy, prevents potential 3-3 budget ties, and avoids special-election expenses.
Applications may be more accessible than financing a special-election campaign.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer filling the seat or hold a special election rather than running a rushed 30-day virtual-only appointment while City Hall is closed.
side_b_arguments: Virtual-only applications and interviews exclude working-class residents lacking computers, bandwidth, or financial stability during the pandemic.
Six members form a full quorum for the budget, and staff capacity should remain focused on COVID-19 relief.
Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People formally requested a special election.
disagreements.resolution: Approved 5-2 by roll call (subsequently rescinded unanimously on April 20 in favor of N.C.G.S. § 160A-63).

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Steve Schewel on March 5, 2020, the Durham City Council work session opened with a unanimous 6-0 voice vote granting an excused absence to Council Member Vernetta Alston and condolences from Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton to the family of North Carolina Central University student-athlete Trevor Van Dyke following recent gun violence. Council pulled consent and budget items for discussion—including Boards and Commissions reports, FY 2021 budget guidelines, council budget requests, Community Conversations contracts, a Forest Hills Neighborhood Protection Overlay initiation, and an Eno River water-supply reclassification resolution—and reviewed wording on the 7-cent BID tax rate, the 30.83-cent General Fund tax rate, and stormwater fee language. In an afternoon deliberation over narrowing roughly $1.3 million in recurring council-initiated budget requests, Mayor Schewel and Council Member Middleton favored immediately cutting a proposed $450,000 trash-can cleaning contract for justice-involved employment via a quick thumbs-up/down filter, whereas Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson favored a hybrid filter and using the non-paired staff scorecard; Council agreed to complete individual scorecards before finalizing cuts. The session concluded with a unanimous 6-0 voice vote settling the upcoming regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Excused Absence for Council Member Vernetta Alston, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the work session to order at 1:00 p.m., with six members present (Mayor Schewel, Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson, and Council Members Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece). Council unanimously approved an excused absence for Council Member Vernetta Alston by voice vote. Council Member Middleton praised Mayor Schewel's State of the City address and offered condolences to NCCU students and the family of Trevor Van Dyke after his fatal shooting, recommitting Council to combatting gun violence.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items, Consent Agenda Review, and Public Hearing Scheduling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Attorney and City Clerk reported no priority items, and Council pulled Consent Items 2 (Boards, Committees, and Commissions reports), 3 (FY 2021 Budget Guidelines), 4 (Initial Discussion of Council Budget Requests), 5 (Community Conversations contract), 6 (Forest Hills Neighborhood Protection Overlay initiation), 10 (Eno River water-supply reclassification support resolution), and 13; Council Member DeDreana Freeman also thanked staff for advancing Item 14 in her neighborhood. Public Hearing Items 17–22 included the FY 2021 Budget and CIP, annexations (Falls Village North Conservation, Fox Crossing, South Mineral Springs and Pleasant), the NCCU Student Center building, and UDO text amendments for Neighborhood Protection Overlay revisions, with a speaker advised that public hearing comments occur at Monday night's regular meeting.

agenda_items.title: Citizens' Matters: Chris Tiffany (Coronavirus Testing)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: During Citizens' Matters at 1:00 p.m., resident Chris Tiffany raised concerns regarding potential false positives in coronavirus diagnostic testing. Following public comment, Mayor Steve Schewel clarified for listeners that health authorities had noted no appreciable concern about false positives.

agenda_items.title: Procedures Committee Follow-Up and Item 3: FY 2021 Budget Development Guidelines
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council noted the need to schedule another Procedures Committee meeting and reviewed Item 3 with Budget Director Bertha Johnson ahead of Monday night's presentation. Members confirmed the Business Improvement District (BID) tax rate remained listed at 7 cents pending tax administration figures and City Manager discussions without being locked in, refined General Fund tax rate wording around the 30.83-cent rate unless Council deems an increase necessary, and asked staff to clarify whether the 50-cent-per-month cap on stormwater fees referred to the increase or the total rate.

agenda_items.title: Item 4: Prioritization Process and Scorecard for Council-Initiated Budget Requests
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle portion of the meeting, Council reviewed evaluation attributes—strategic alignment, equity, one-time versus recurring funding frequency, and administrative staffing impact—for roughly $1.3 million in recurring council-initiated budget requests. Mayor Steve Schewel and Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton advocated trimming the list immediately and dropping a $450,000 trash-can cleaning contract intended to hire justice-involved workers, arguing the City should invest directly in justice-involved programming rather than municipal trash-can cleaning. Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson suggested a hybrid filter and favored using the individual non-paired scorecard consistent with staff practice; Council agreed each member would score all items with staff documentation.

agenda_items.title: Settling the Agenda for Upcoming Regular City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager recommended settling the upcoming regular meeting agenda with Consent Items 1–3 and 5–16 and GBA Public Hearings Items 17–22. Council approved settling the agenda unanimously by voice vote and adjourned at 4:28 p.m.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for Council Member Vernetta Alston
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote among the six seated members present at roll call; Vernetta Alston excused absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member Vernetta Alston requested an excused absence prior to the meeting.

disagreements.meeting_title: City Council Work Session
disagreements.issue: Method and Criteria for Filtering Council-Initiated Budget Requests
disagreements.summary: Council members differed over whether to eliminate certain council-initiated budget requests immediately via an informal thumbs-up/down vote—specifically a $450,000 trash-can cleaning contract—or use a structured scorecard rubric after reviewing documentation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Eliminate non-essential or mismatched proposals upfront via quick thumbs-up/down screening, including removing the $450,000 trash-can cleaning contract.
side_a_arguments: Municipal government should not provide private trash-can cleaning services.
If Council wants to spend $450,000 on justice-involved employment, it should invest directly in targeted justice-involved programs rather than an external cleaning vendor.
disagreements.side_b_position: Use a hybrid yes/no/maybe filter alongside the standard non-paired staff scorecard so members can evaluate reduced amounts, equity, and recurring costs systematically.
side_b_arguments: The non-paired scorecard aligns with the evaluation framework already used by City staff.
A structured scorecard lets members register support at lower funding levels or after reviewing full project documentation.
disagreements.resolution: Council agreed that Budget staff would distribute individual non-paired scorecards and full project documentation for every member to complete and return.

meetings.title: Durham City Council March 2, 2020 (with closed captions)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the March 2, 2020 City Council meeting with his State of the City address, highlighting the McDougall Terrace carbon monoxide crisis, the $95 million affordable housing bond, DEAR and Welcome Home second-chance programs, and honoring city frontline staff, 911 dispatchers, and April 10 explosion first responders. After approving the consent agenda 7-0 (excluding pulled Item 5) and voting 7-0 in two motions to add six Police Gang Unit positions (Item 17), council passed the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force bylaws (Item 22) 6-1—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and Mark-Anthony Middleton voting Nay over acting before Durham County review. In public hearings, council unanimously approved 7-0 the 3871 Guess Road FLUM amendment and IL(D) self-storage rezoning with a 30-acre conservation easement (Item 18), and approved the 3516 Glen Road Townhomes annexation (Item 19) 6-1—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting Nay over rural character impacts—before approving the accompanying utility extension, consistency statement, and PDR 7.042 zoning 7-0. Council closed the session by approving the Urban Avenue street closing and Beltline easement agreement (Item 20) 7-0 and the $180,000 Legal Aid DEAR contract (Item 5) 7-0.

agenda_items.title: State of the City Address and Recognition of Frontline City Heroes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel delivered his 2020 State of the City address reflecting on the April 10, 2019 Brightleaf gas explosion, the relocation of 280 McDougall Terrace families, the $95 million affordable housing bond, gun violence trends, and the DEAR and Welcome Home reentry programs. He honored the Impact Team, 911 dispatcher Emily Battello, and firefighters and police officers who responded to the Brightleaf blast, followed by Jordan High School chorus music.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 5) and Public Comment on McDougall Terrace
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the consent agenda 7-0 (excluding Item 5, Legal Aid of North Carolina contract, pulled for public comment). Speakers including Mr. Zayiti, Victoria Peterson, and Jackie Wagstaff criticized Durham Housing Authority leadership, asbestos concerns, and volunteer recognition regarding McDougall Terrace.

agenda_items.title: Item 17: Durham Police Department Gang Unit Staffing (Six Full-Time Positions)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Minister Paul Scott, Mr. Zayiti, and Victoria Peterson raised concerns about criminalizing Black youth, police gang databases, and the need for economic and vocational training alongside policing. Council Member Freeman noted the Chief's program aims to offer pathways out of gangs before council voted 7-0 to authorize six full-time gang unit positions and 7-0 to recognize the associated costs.

agenda_items.title: Item 22: Community Safety and Wellness Task Force Bylaws
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham Beyond Policing speaker Danielle Purefoy supported expanding justice-involved and youth seats on the task force and funding non-police response research. Council Member Middleton objected to any three-year police hiring moratorium and opposed adopting bylaws before Durham County commissioners held a hearing (while Freeman also voiced concern over county buy-in), whereas Council Member Alston and Mayor Schewel argued passing the bylaws invites county action; the motion passed 6-1 with Middleton voting No.

agenda_items.title: Item 18: Public Hearing — 3871 Guess Road FLUM Amendment and Rezoning (PDR 2.00 to IL(D))
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Emily Struthers presented the request for a 10.14-acre portion of a 40-acre parcel at 3871 Guess Rd. to build a 150,000 sq. ft. two-story self-storage facility with a 30-acre permanent conservation easement and $10,000 affordable housing proffer, noting the Planning Commission recommended denial 10-2. Despite opposition over excess storage facilities, a commercial-node 'loophole,' and wetland/buffer limits, council approved the FLUM amendment, consistency statement, and UDO rezoning in three 7-0 votes.

agenda_items.title: Item 19: Public Hearing — 3516 Glen Road Townhomes Annexation, Utility Agreement, and Rezoning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Jamie Sunyak and applicant attorney Bahati Mutisya presented a 52.508-acre non-contiguous annexation and rezoning from Rural Residential to PDR 7.042 for up to 279 townhomes capped at 1,700 heated square feet, with 25% alley-loaded units, $41,850 for the affordable housing fund, $4,500 for DPS, and a 5-foot privacy fence (Planning Commission approved 7-5). Council Member Freeman opposed annexing dense townhomes into a rural community lacking conservation advocacy (voting Nay on annexation 6-1), before council approved the utility agreement, consistency statement, and rezoning 7-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-1 (Annexation, Freeman Nay); Passed 7-0 (UEA, Consistency, Zoning)

agenda_items.title: Item 20: Public Hearing — Urban Avenue Street Closing and Beltline Development/Easement Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Pat Young, General Services' Stacey Poston, Patrick Byker, and Braham Specialty president Mercer Stanfield presented closing 934.31 linear feet of Urban Ave. in exchange for 100 linear feet of Beltline trail construction, 15 public parking spaces, and $30,979 cash ($174,219 total value). Mayor Pro Tem Johnson and Council Members Caballero and Freeman questioned 'even trade' land swaps and surrounding Beltline gentrification before voting 7-0 to approve both the street closing and the easement agreement with JACO 949 Washington Investors LLC.

agenda_items.title: Item 5 (Pulled Consent): Legal Aid of North Carolina DEAR Program Contract
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson questioned why the $180,000 Legal Aid contract for the Durham Expunction and Restoration (DEAR) program did not go through an RFP and urged Legal Aid to continue representing McDougall Terrace tenants. Council then voted 7-0 to approve Item 5 and adjourned.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council March 2, 2020 (with closed captions)
disagreements.issue: Timing of Adopting Community Safety and Wellness Task Force Bylaws Without Prior County Action
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to adopt bylaws for the joint Community Safety and Wellness Task Force over Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton's objection that Durham County commissioners had not yet held a hearing or committed to participate.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the revised task force bylaws now to signal city commitment and invite Durham County and Durham Public Schools to join.
side_a_arguments: Bylaws already incorporated input from county, school, and court stakeholders.
Passing the bylaws puts constructive pressure on the county to act and does not preclude future amendments.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer voting on joint bylaws until Durham County has reviewed and indicated willingness to participate, and reject any moratorium on police hiring.
side_b_arguments: Passing bylaws naming the county while county commissioners are in an election cycle and have not vetted the document shows lack of inter-board courtesy.
A three-year moratorium on hiring police officers proposed in the Durham Beyond Policing document is irresponsible for a city approaching 300,000 residents.
disagreements.resolution: Motion to adopt the task force bylaws passed 6-1, with Middleton casting the sole Nay vote (Freeman voiced reservations about county buy-in during debate but voted Aye).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council March 2, 2020 (with closed captions)
disagreements.issue: Non-Contiguous Annexation of 279 Townhomes at 3516 Glen Road
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to annex 52.508 acres on Glen Road for a 279-unit townhome development, with Council Member DeDreana Freeman dissenting over incompatibility with surrounding rural homes and unequal land-conservation leverage.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the satellite annexation and townhome rezoning because it meets annexation policy, matches the Medium Density Residential FLUM, and includes strong affordability commitments.
side_a_arguments: Capping units at 1,700 heated square feet promotes natural affordability alongside $41,850 for the affordable housing fund and 25% alley-loaded design.
Developer conducted extensive community outreach and added a privacy fence proffer.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose annexing dense townhomes into a rural area of small single-family and mobile homes where residents lacked the resources to secure conservation concessions.
side_b_arguments: Dense two-story townhomes diverge sharply from neighboring rural and manufactured-home residences.
Unlike Guess Road, where affluent environmental advocates secured 30 acres of conservation, lower-income Glen Road neighbors lacked equal leverage.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation passed 6-1 (Freeman Nay); subsequent utility extension agreement, consistency statement, and PDR 7.042 zoning passed 7-0.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting - Budget Retreat
meetings.executive_summary: Although cataloged as the February 28, 2020 Special City Council Meeting - Budget Retreat, the Granicus transcript digest for city_granicus_2428 actually contains the recording of Day 1 of the FY 2020–21 Budget Retreat held on February 14, 2020 (explicitly referencing Valentine's Day and previewing the upcoming February 28 retreat with Dr. Sandy Darity and Dr. Michael Walden). Budget Director Bertha Johnson opened with an overview of resident survey and focus-group engagement, Comprehensive Plan coordination, IdeaStarter finalists, department director briefings, multi-year financial projections, and capital improvement planning, alongside zero-waste composting logistics. City Manager Tom Bonfield welcomed new leadership hires—including Assistant Budget Director Monica and Transportation Director Sean—recognized retiring Parks and Recreation Director Rhonda Parker, and reflected on his 12th Durham budget cycle since 2009. Following a truncated middle section, Council members debated how council-originated budget items (such as a $50,000 boards-and-commissions stipend request) should be vetted, reaching informal consensus without a formal vote to pilot requiring standard staff budget forms, colleague notification, and work-session placement before staff investment.

agenda_items.title: Opening Logistics and FY 2020–21 Budget Retreat Overview (Digest Mirrors Feb. 14 Day 1 Recording)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff opened the retreat with zero-waste composting and recycling instructions, and Budget Director Bertha Johnson thanked budget staff, department directors, and interpreters before outlining the retreat agenda. Notably, the transcript digest attached to this February 28 catalog record reflects the February 14, 2020 Day 1 retreat—referencing Valentine's Day, Pat Young's transit/rail briefing, IdeaStarter finalists, multi-year financial projections, and previewing Dr. Sandy Darity's racial wealth gap talk, Dr. Michael Walden's economic outlook, dedicated housing fund, transit/parking, and Participatory Budgeting evaluation scheduled for February 28.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Opening Remarks, Leadership Welcomes, and Retirement Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield thanked department heads and staff for budget preparation, welcomed new officials including Assistant Budget Director Monica and Transportation Director Sean, and recognized Parks and Recreation Director Rhonda Parker ahead of her late-February retirement. Drawing on journals from his 12 budget cycles since winter 2009, Bonfield framed recurring fiscal and community priorities shaping the FY 2020–21 budget.

agenda_items.title: Deliberation on Process for Council-Initiated Budget Requests
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle portion of the 7.5-hour session, Council members discussed how council-originated spending ideas—citing a $50,000 boards-and-commissions stipend proposal from the Procedures Committee and Clerk's office—should enter the budget workflow. Several members objected to proposals appearing unexpectedly in budget drafts without full-council awareness and urged vetting ideas at a work session first, while others emphasized timely submission on standard department forms. Members agreed informally to pilot a transparent workflow requiring standard staff forms, peer notice, and work-session discussion, and closed by affirming their commitment to collaborate even when disagreeing.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Steve Schewel with all seven seated members present at opening roll call on February 20, 2020, the Durham City Council approved the City Manager's priority items (referring Item 13 back to staff, adding a Citizens' Matters attachment, and carrying over Item 22 on Community Safety Task Force bylaws) and the Clerk's/Attorney's priority item (referring Item 2 back to staff) by unanimous 7-0 voice votes. During Citizens' Matters, a speaker addressed toxic hazards including carbon monoxide and mold confirmed by Durham Housing Authority Executive Director Anthony Scott at McDougall Terrace, and Assistant Budget Director Monica Croskey-Chabota briefed Council on Legal Aid of North Carolina assuming 12-month management of the Durham Expunction and Restoration (DEAR) program. Following a truncated middle section and a briefing on the Parks Foundation and inclusive playground swing fundraising, Council debated Item 22's draft 15-member Community Safety Task Force bylaws—specifically balancing policy/legal seats against representation from justice-involved and over-policed neighborhoods and whether to adopt bylaws before Durham County Commissioners formally vetted or committed to them—without taking a vote on the bylaws. Council closed by unanimously settling the upcoming regular meeting agenda by voice vote after receiving a text update from DHA's Anthony Scott raising the count of ready units to 14.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Announcements, and Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the work session to order with all seven seated members present; Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson introduced Duke intern Kit Devine, Council Member Javiera Caballero noted she might depart early due to a snow day, and a member apologized for missing a Black History Month proclamation while noting outreach on HB 40/SB 283 reparations study bills. Council voted 7-0 by voice to approve the City Manager's priority items (referring Item 13 back to staff, adding attachment 2 to Item 21, and carrying over Item 22 on Community Safety Task Force bylaws) and voted 7-0 by voice to approve the Clerk's priority referral of Item 2 back to staff.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review and Citizens' Matters on McDougall Terrace
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read through Administrative Consent Items 1–15—including DPAC Oversight Committee reappointment, user access audit, Families Moving Forward CDBG contracts, FY 2019 Q2 financial report, WeWork swing space at 300 Morris Street, StayWell wellness contract, and street paving amendments—with only Item 5 pulled for discussion. During Citizens' Matters, a speaker criticized conditions at McDougall Terrace after DHA Executive Director Anthony Scott confirmed carbon monoxide, mold, and other hazards at the city's oldest public housing complex.

agenda_items.title: Item 5: Legal Aid of North Carolina Contract for DEAR Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant Budget Director Monica Croskey-Chabota answered questions from Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson regarding Legal Aid of North Carolina assuming responsibility for the Durham Expunction and Restoration (DEAR) program. She noted judicial support from Judges Reinhardt, Jones, and Hall in waiving old traffic tickets and explained that current funding covers 12 months while the DEAR advisory board works to diversify funding sources before fiscal-year funding expires.

agenda_items.title: Durham Parks Foundation Commemorations and Accessible Playground Swing Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle portion of the transcript covering the Parks Foundation five-year report and Police Gang Unit update, discussion highlighted commemorative park benches, a Grant Hill key-to-the-city event, and efforts to replace an expensive inclusive playground swing with roughly 50% of funds raised via the Morehead Hill Neighborhood Association and Neighborhood Improvement Services matching support.

agenda_items.title: Item 22: Community Safety Task Force Bylaws Deliberation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members examined draft bylaws for the 15-member Community Safety Task Force, debating whether the seat distribution overweighted policy and legal professionals relative to justice-involved residents and people living in over-policed neighborhoods. Members also raised concerns that Durham County Commissioners had not yet vetted or committed to participating, and discussed passing the City's draft bylaws while formally inviting the County Commission and Durham Public Schools Board of Education to review and propose amendments, noting precedents like the Environmental Affairs Board and Cultural Advisory Board.

agenda_items.title: EBOP Bidder Workforce Statistics, Settling the Agenda, and McDougall Terrace Unit Count
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council briefly reviewed the purpose of collecting contractor employee demographic statistics alongside the Equal Business Opportunity Program (EBOP) since 2000. Council unanimously approved settling the upcoming regular meeting agenda by voice vote, relayed a text update from DHA Executive Director Anthony Scott noting 8 additional units were ready (bringing the total from 6 to 14), and adjourned at 4:04 p.m.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Feb 17, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the February 17, 2020 meeting, the Durham City Council recognized Patricia Obregon with the Neighbor Spotlight award and proclaimed Samaritan Health Center Day before moving Item 17 (right-of-way withdrawal ordinance) onto the consent agenda and voting on consent items 1–11 and 17. Later in the evening, Council held an extended deliberation on the Kendrick Estates annexation and zoning application, where members divided over stormwater flooding risks, upstream mitigation by Trinity School, and the enforceability of developer commitments in an annexation. Council narrowly approved the annexation ordinance, consistency statement, and zoning ordinance in three consecutive 4-3 votes, with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye, and DeDreana Freeman, Charlie Reece, and Javiera Caballero voting Nay.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Ceremonial Recognitions (Neighbor Spotlight and Samaritan Health Center Day)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order, Cub Scout Pack 424 from Immaculate Conception Church led the Pledge of Allegiance, and all seven council members answered roll call. Council presented the February 2020 Neighbor Spotlight award to Patricia Obregon of Old East Durham for organizing Spanish-language computer classes and participatory budgeting outreach, and issued a proclamation honoring Samaritan Health Center Day.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and Priority Item Repositioning (Item 17)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton announced he had brought on a council intern, and Council Member DeDreana Freeman promoted youth workforce site sign-ups and upcoming Carolina Theatre and Durham Parks and Recreation summer youth programming. The City Manager reported one priority item, repositioning Item 17 (ordinance amending Durham City Code provisions regulating withdrawal of right-of-way) from a public hearing to the consent agenda because no public hearing was required.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1–11 and 17)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the consent agenda, which included an interlocal agreement with Durham County for an unsheltered coordinating agency, a tenant-based rental assistance contract with the Durham Housing Authority, six replacement transit vehicles, the Triangle Bikeway Implementation Study, mutual aid agreements with Cary and Chapel Hill, stormwater lab testing, HVAC integration, and Item 17. Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson commented without pulling Item 9 (SAS Institute smart building analytics expansion) that she and Mayor Schewel had met with SAS regarding DHS/ICE contract concerns.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (vote closed at 00:21:58; tally truncated in digest)

agenda_items.title: Kendrick Estates Annexation, Consistency Statement, and Zoning Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After closing the continued public hearing on Baker Residential's Kendrick Estates annexation adjacent to a park, Council questioned the developer (Mark Bowles) and staff on proffer enforceability, a proposed 5-foot black aluminum fence versus an 8-foot opaque fence, public cul-de-sac parking for trailhead access, and pre-existing stormwater flooding near Trinity School. Mayor Schewel moved approval, arguing annexation imposed stricter 100-year stormwater standards and satisfied environmental board requests, while Council Members DeDreana Freeman, Charlie Reece, and Javiera Caballero opposed moving forward amid unresolved downstream flooding and enforceability concerns. All three motions passed 4-3.

votes.item_title: Kendrick Estates: Adopt Ordinance to Annex and Extend City Limits
votes.notes: Clerk announced 'The motion passes four to three with council members Freeman, Reece and Caballero voting no' (ASR rendered 'no' as 'now').
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Schewel moved adoption of the annexation ordinance, noting the developer agreed to reissue its commitment letter to include a 5-foot fence along the park boundary and that city annexation brings 100-year stormwater treatment standards. Council Members Freeman, Reece, and Caballero voted no due to ongoing flooding concerns and lack of binding development plan enforcement in an annexation.

votes.item_title: Kendrick Estates: Adopt Consistency Statement
votes.notes: Passed 4-3 with Caballero, Freeman, and Reece voting no.
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted on the statutory consistency statement accompanying the Kendrick Estates rezoning.

votes.item_title: Kendrick Estates: Adopt Zoning Ordinance
votes.notes: Passed 4-3 with Caballero, Freeman, and Reece voting no; meeting adjourned at 9:53 PM.
votes.discussion_detail: Final motion to adopt the zoning ordinance for Kendrick Estates following the annexation and consistency votes.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Feb 17, 2020 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Kendrick Estates Annexation, Stormwater Flooding Risks, and Enforceability of Developer Commitments
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 over whether to approve Baker Residential's Kendrick Estates annexation and zoning request near an adjacent park and downstream flood-prone properties, weighing city 100-year stormwater rules and housing supply against unmitigated flooding risks and non-binding annexation commitments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve annexation and zoning because city development brings stricter 100-year stormwater treatment, adds housing supply, and incorporates park-buffer commitments.
side_a_arguments: Leaving the site unannexed in Durham County could produce a worse stormwater outcome than annexing under the city's 100-year stormwater treatment standard.

The developer addressed concerns from Durham Advocates for Sustainability, New Hope Audubon, Friends of the Park, and the Environmental Affairs Board, and agreed to reissue a commitment letter including a 5-foot fence.
Durham needs additional housing supply.
disagreements.side_b_position: Opposed moving forward due to pre-existing downstream flooding, lack of legally enforceable proffers in an annexation, and preference to await Trinity School's drainage mitigation.
side_b_arguments: Commitments made in a letter during an annexation are not legally enforceable by the city the way a rezoning development plan is.
Building should not proceed where known flooding exists without first seeing the results of Trinity School's upstream channel mitigation.
Unannexed, the parcel would yield far fewer homes on larger lots with significantly lower stormwater impact.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation ordinance, consistency statement, and zoning ordinance all passed 4-3.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting - Budget Retreat
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council convened Day 1 of its FY 2020–21 Budget Retreat on February 14, 2020, opening with zero-waste meeting logistics and a comprehensive roadmap presented by Budget Director Bertha Johnson covering resident surveys, focus groups, Comprehensive Plan engagement, transit updates from Pat Young, IdeaStarter finalists, department budget presentations, and multi-year financial and CIP forecasts. City Manager Tom Bonfield welcomed newly appointed leaders including Assistant Budget Director Monica and Transportation Director Sean, honored retiring Parks and Recreation Director Rhonda Parker, and reflected on fiscal themes across his 12 Durham budgets since 2009. Following a truncated middle portion of the 7.5-hour session, Council members debated how council-initiated spending proposals—such as a $50,000 boards-and-commissions stipend request—should be introduced and vetted. No formal votes were taken, but members reached informal consensus to pilot requiring standard staff budget forms, colleague notification, and work-session placement before advancing council-initiated budget items.

agenda_items.title: Zero-Waste Logistics and FY 2020–21 Budget Retreat Agenda Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff introduced composting and waste-reduction procedures for the retreat, and Budget Director Bertha Johnson thanked budget staff, department directors, and volunteer Spanish interpreter Anne Parrish. Johnson outlined Day 1 topics—resident survey and focus-group feedback, Comprehensive Plan coordination, transit and rail updates by Pat Young, IdeaStarter finalists, department director sessions, and multi-year/CIP projections—while previewing February 28 presentations by Dr. Sandy Darity on the racial wealth gap, Dr. Michael Walden on the economic outlook, dedicated housing funds, transit/parking, and Participatory Budgeting evaluation.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Opening Remarks, Leadership Welcomes, and Retirement Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield recognized department heads for their budget preparation, welcomed Assistant Budget Director Monica and Transportation Director Sean to their first Durham budget retreat, and paid tribute to retiring Parks and Recreation Director Rhonda Parker. Drawing on journals dating back to winter 2009 across his 12 Durham budget cycles, Bonfield highlighted long-term themes guiding the upcoming FY 2020–21 budget.

agenda_items.title: Deliberation on Process for Council-Initiated Budget Requests
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After a truncated middle section, Council members debated transparency and workflow around council-initiated budget requests, citing a $50,000 boards-and-commissions stipend item stemming from the Procedures Committee and Clerk's office. Members voiced concern about requests entering budget drafts behind the scenes without full-council vetting and agreed informally to pilot a process requiring members to submit standard staff forms, inform all colleagues, and bring requests to a work session for collective deliberation.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Steve Schewel on February 6, 2020 with a four-member quorum (Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson and Council Members Vernetta Alston and Javiera Caballero present; Council Members Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece excused for School of Government training and National League of Cities), the Durham City Council reviewed consent items, public comments, transit updates, and sign-ordinance revisions without recording formal votes. During Citizens' Matters, speakers criticized Council's 2018 resolution regarding Israeli police training, raised McDougall Terrace resident access issues and law-enforcement relations, and urged action regarding the Mayor Pro Tem office; Council also heard from Durham Beyond Policing proposing revisions to the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force bylaws to broaden partnership with the County and School Board. Finance Director David Boyd explained reallocations of excess funds from closed CIP projects, and transportation staff presented the Durham County Transit Plan and commuter rail risk assessment, noting schedule constraints on requested equitable engagement and a 13% regional funding gap. Finally, City Attorney staff (Don O'Toole) and Planning staff (Michael Stock) briefed Council on 18 months of Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) sign revisions required for content neutrality under Reed v. Town of Gilbert—including temporary signs in the right-of-way—ahead of Monday night's public hearing.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Consent Agenda Pulls, and Citizens' Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the work session to order with four members present (Schewel, Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson, Vernetta Alston, and Javiera Caballero) and three excused absences (Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece). Council pulled Consent Items 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, and Supplemental Item 21 (Community Safety Task Force Bylaws), with public comment on Item 16 (UDO Signs) deferred to Monday night's public hearing. During Citizens' Matters, Catherine Wolf criticized the April 2018 resolution on police training in Israel, another speaker discussed McDougall Terrace access and law enforcement trust, and a speaker criticized the Mayor Pro Tempore.

agenda_items.title: Triangle Bikeway Study, FY 2019–20 CIP Close-Out, and Community Safety Task Force Bylaws
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council briefly addressed Housing Choice Voucher restrictions at subsidized developments like Acra and commuting options on the Triangle Bikeway (Item 5). Finance Director David Boyd walked through Item 6 (FY 2019–20 CIP budget amendment project close-out), explaining how leftover balances from closed capital projects are either reallocated to active/new projects or returned to debt-model capacity for upcoming CIP planning. A representative of Durham Beyond Policing then submitted proposed revisions to the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force bylaws (Item 21) envisioning a broader partnership with Durham Beyond Policing, the City, the County, and the School Board.

agenda_items.title: Item 15: Durham County Transit Plan and Commuter Rail Risk Assessment Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle portion of the meeting, transportation staff presented an FTA-style risk assessment for the regional commuter rail study and a proposed memorandum of understanding among project partners including railroads. Staff noted that the project management team declined to replicate Durham's full equitable community engagement process due to schedule constraints, and flagged a 13% regional funding gap beyond Durham's 20% planned share while noting Durham County residents were projected to make up 25% to 30% of commuter rail ridership.

agenda_items.title: Item 16: UDO Text Amendment – Sign Ordinance Revisions (Reed v. Town of Gilbert)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant City Attorney Don O'Toole and Planning staffer Michael Stock presented UDO sign ordinance amendments developed over 18 months to comply with the U.S. Supreme Court's content-neutrality ruling in Reed v. Town of Gilbert. The proposal preserves time, place, and manner rules, creates non-commercial sign budgets on residential parcels with extra commercial sign allowances during sales, codifies temporary roadside fatality memorials (such as ghost bikes) for 45 days, and addresses temporary signs in public rights-of-way outside election periods—an area flagged by Council Members Charlie Reece and Vernetta Alston following feedback from the Realtors Association—ahead of Monday night's public hearing.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Feb 3, 2020 (with closed captions)
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Charlie Reece on an excused absence, the six present members of the Durham City Council met on February 3, 2020 and unanimously granted excused work-session absences for DeDreana Freeman and Mark-Anthony Middleton (6-0) while postponing Item 3 (Community Safety Task Force bylaws) to Thursday's work session at Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson's request. Council approved the remaining consent agenda items 6-0, including a non-sworn classification and compensation study amendment and participatory budgeting technology funding for Durham Public Schools. The bulk of the meeting focused on emotional public comments regarding the McDougall Terrace public housing carbon monoxide and mold crisis, with residents demanding accountability, rent refunds, and clearer relocation timelines. Council then took up the two pulled consent items—approving the Legal Aid of North Carolina eviction diversion grant contract (6-0) and the shared active transportation report and e-scooter ordinance revision (6-0).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Excused Absences for Work Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order and Cub Scout Pack 451 from Westminster Presbyterian Church led the Pledge of Allegiance. Six council members were present, with Charlie Reece on a pre-approved excused absence; Council immediately voted 6-0 to approve excused absences for DeDreana Freeman and Mark-Anthony Middleton for the upcoming Thursday work session.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and Consent Agenda Deferral Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Freeman noted her UNC School of Government leadership training and urged community volunteers to interview students for the Durham Youth Internship Program. Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson requested postponing Item 3 (Community Safety Task Force bylaws) to Thursday's work session so community authors could review them, and praised increased eviction diversion funding while noting it still covers only about 10% of eligible tenants.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 6–10, 12–13; Items 3, 4, and 5 Pulled/Deferred)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Item 3 (Community Safety Task Force bylaws) was deferred to Thursday's work session, Item 4 (Legal Aid eviction diversion contract) was pulled by resident Waldo Fenner, and Item 5 (shared active transportation report and ordinance revision) was pulled by resident Mimi Kessler. Council unanimously approved the remaining items (bid report, Series 2020 fleet financing, Sandy Creek Drive land lease, non-sworn compensation study amendment, DUHS grant, ESRI software maintenance, and Participatory Budgeting DPS technology funding).

agenda_items.title: McDougall Terrace Public Comments and Durham Housing Authority Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Residents and advocates—including Wilma Liverpool, Ms. Molina, and Mr. Green—described McDougall Terrace as a humanitarian crisis caused by years of deferred maintenance, carbon monoxide leaks, mold, and failed HUD inspections, calling for tenant rent refunds and alternative housing placements. Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton and DHA Director Anthony Scott responded, noting buildings would reopen incrementally only once verified safe without prematurely guessing return dates.

agenda_items.title: Item 4: Grant Contract with Legal Aid of North Carolina (Eviction Diversion)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel noted that while state or federal funding would be preferable, local government was stepping up to fund Legal Aid of North Carolina's eviction diversion representation for Durham residents. Council moved, seconded, and approved the contract unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Item 5: Shared Active Transportation Report and Ordinance Revision (E-Scooters)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Mimi Kessler raised safety and survey concerns regarding shared active transportation (e-scooters) and asked about driver liability. Senior Assistant City Attorney Fred Lamar clarified that motorist liability for hitting a scooter rider follows the same fault-based standard as hitting a bicyclist or skateboarder, and Mayor Schewel affirmed Council would continue monitoring scooter safety closely before approving the item 6-0.

votes.notes: Charlie Reece absent (excused). Passed 6-0 at 01:15:14; meeting adjourned at 8:14 PM.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Steve Schewel on January 23, 2020, the Durham City Council work session opened with a unanimous 6-0 voice vote excusing Council Member Charlie Reece due to a family illness and a 6-0 voice vote approving the City Manager's referral of Item 11 (police-initiated non-consensual towing fees) back to staff. During Citizens' Matters, speakers criticized police gatekeeping at public meetings, urged Durham to file an amicus brief and pass a resolution opposing the RDU Airport Authority's proposed Odd Fellows Tract rock quarry and 8.3-mile barbed-wire fence (with Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson and Council indicating deference to Wake County and Raleigh leadership unless requested), and addressed McDougall Terrace. Transportation staff briefed Council on Shared Active Transportation (Item 5) ordinance updates shifting scooter permits from annual to monthly payments and funding scooter corrals, prompting Council questions on demographic equity, unbanked riders, street-parking conversions, and cost recovery. Following an update on NCCU's upcoming Participatory Budgeting evaluation, Council voted 6-0 by voice to add McDougall Terrace public comments as a recurring item on regular Monday night agendas until all residents return home, and voted 6-0 to settle the upcoming regular agenda.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Excused Absence for Charlie Reece, Announcements, and Priority Referral
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the work session to order with six members present, and Council voted 6-0 by voice to grant Council Member Charlie Reece an excused absence due to family illness. Council Member DeDreana Freeman announced YouthWorks interview dates (April 13–23) toward a goal of 1,000 youth opportunities and urged colleagues to sign up for interview slots. Council then voted 6-0 by voice to approve the City Manager's priority item referring Agenda Item 11 (Ordinance No. 14379 non-consensual police-initiated towing fees) back to the administration.

agenda_items.title: Administrative Consent Agenda Review and Citizens' Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Consent Items 3, 4 (Legal Aid eviction-defense grant contract), 5 (Shared Active Transportation report and ordinance revision), and 13 (Participatory Budgeting DPS technology funding) from an agenda that also included fleet financing, a Sandy Creek Drive lease, non-sworn compensation study amendments, and Esri software maintenance. During Citizens' Matters, Chris Tiffany objected to police presence and bus-access barriers at meetings, Tanya Meyer and Dr. Spencer urged Durham to file an amicus brief and oppose RDU Airport Authority's Odd Fellows Tract quarry and 8.3-mile security fence (with Council explaining it would follow Wake County's lead unless Wake County officials asked Durham to weigh in), and Andrea Muffin-Hudson spoke prior to McDougall Terrace comments in a truncated segment.

agenda_items.title: Item 5: Shared Active Transportation (Scooters) Report and Ordinance Revision
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle section, Transportation staff (including Bill Judge) outlined ordinance revisions moving scooter permits from annual to monthly fees to match seasonal demand and using permit revenue for painted scooter corrals and stencils. Council members pressed staff on tracking equity beyond the 20% census-tract deployment rule—asking about user demographics, unbanked payment options, converting downtown street parking spots to scooter parking with ParkDurham, and ensuring permit fees recoup City staff costs rather than subsidizing privileged riders.

agenda_items.title: Item 13: Participatory Budgeting Evaluation Update (NCCU MPA)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget and Management Services staffer Andrew reported that North Carolina Central University's Master of Public Administration program was evaluating the City's Participatory Budgeting cycle, with the written report due February 7 and findings scheduled for presentation at the February 28 budget retreat.

agenda_items.title: Recurring McDougall Terrace Public Comment Item, Agenda Settlement, and Procedures
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following procedural guidance from staff attorney/clerk representative Carmisha, Council voted 6-0 by voice to add McDougall Terrace public comments as a recurring item on regular Monday night City Council agendas until all residents are back in their homes. Council then voted 6-0 to settle the upcoming regular meeting agenda (Consent Items 3–10, 12, and 13 plus the supplemental McDougall Terrace item), clarified with the Clerk that the 'Other Matters' heading added to regular agendas in 2019 would go to the Procedures Committee, and adjourned at 3:06 p.m.

votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote among the six seated members present at roll call; Charlie Reece absent.

votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote; Charlie Reece absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Referred Item 11 (amendment to Ordinance No. 14379 establishing non-consensual police-initiated towing fees) back to administration for further work.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Jan 21, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: On January 21, 2020, the Durham City Council presented the Neighbor Spotlight award to Natalie Spring, heard a Sister Cities delegation preview for Tilarán, Costa Rica, and proclaimed Fred Korematsu Day of Civil Liberties and the Constitution before unanimously approving a 14-item consent agenda (7-0) that included an interlocal agreement with the Durham Housing Authority for security cameras and lighting. In its sole public hearing, Council unanimously adopted a consistency statement (7-0) and Unified Development Ordinance text amendment (TC1900002, 7-0) allowing recreational outdoor lighting during late hours in industrial districts with a Minor Special Use Permit, enabling a proposed Topgolf mixed-use development at Page Road and I-40. Afterward, Mayor Steve Schewel opened the floor for five McDougall Terrace residents and supporters to share urgent health and housing concerns and highlighted $60 million in housing bond funds for public housing redevelopment.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Ceremonial Recognitions (Natalie Spring, Sister Cities, Fred Korematsu Day)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order with all seven council members present and Scout Troops 450 and 146 leading the Pledge of Allegiance. Council honored Cleveland-Holloway resident Natalie Spring with the January 2020 Neighbor Spotlight award, heard from Brady Searls regarding the Sister Cities delegation to Tilarán, Costa Rica (joined by Council Member Caballero and Mayor Pro Tem Johnson), and issued a proclamation for Fred Korematsu Day accepted by the Japanese American Society of North Carolina.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1–14)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved all 14 consent agenda items in a single vote, including Human Relations Commission appointments, an expedited hearing request for 505 W. Chapel Hill Street, participatory budgeting accessibility ramps, HOPWA and Housing for New Hope contracts, police headquarters elevator maintenance, conveyance of 2404 Lincoln Street, an interlocal agreement with Durham Housing Authority to procure security cameras and lighting, City Hall HVAC/electrical renovations, and ST-303 pavement preservation.

agenda_items.title: Item 17: UDO Text Amendment — Outdoor Lighting (TC1900002)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planner Carl Kolosna presented privately initiated text amendment TC1900002 modifying UDO Section 7.4.2.B.2 to allow late-hour recreational outdoor lighting in IL, IP, and I industrial districts (affecting roughly 3,000 parcels) to remain exempt from Section 7.4 lighting standards if at least 100 feet from residential uses and approved via a Minor Special Use Permit (which can require up to 300 feet separation). Attorney representatives and Todd Waldo of Topgolf explained the change is needed for a 46-acre mixed-use development at Page Road and I-40 expected to generate 1,200 jobs (450–500 at Topgolf); Council Members noted the Planning Commission's 9-4 vote and reservations about using a general text amendment for a single site before approving both motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: McDougall Terrace Public Comment and Housing Redevelopment Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Reversing an earlier plan for an informal post-meeting discussion, Mayor Schewel opened the floor for five signed-up speakers—including Ms. Banner and Ms. Ormond—to describe fever and healthcare barriers in hotels, standing water and mold in apartments, and solidarity with residents. Mayor Schewel explained that return dates remained uncertain pending safety clearance and reiterated that $60 million from the affordable housing bond is dedicated to DHA redevelopment, freeing $7 million in DHA's budget for McDougall Terrace.

votes.item_title: Item 17 (TC1900002): Adopt Consistency Statement for Outdoor Lighting UDO Text Amendment
votes.notes: Passed 7-0 at 00:51:56.
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the consistency statement following staff presentation, Topgolf testimony, and discussion of the Planning Commission's 9-4 recommendation.

votes.item_title: Item 17 (TC1900002): Adopt Ordinance Amending the UDO (Outdoor Lighting Applicability)
votes.notes: Passed 7-0 at 00:52:16.
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the UDO text amendment requiring a Minor Special Use Permit for late-hour recreational lighting in IL, IP, and I industrial zones.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Steve Schewel with all seven seated members present on January 9, 2020, the Durham City Council work session opened by recognizing Technology Solutions staff for raising over $3,000 for the Boys and Girls Club and reviewing consent items including Housing for New Hope outreach contracts, DHA security cameras, and UDO outdoor lighting rules. Citizens' Matters speakers raised Forest Hills Neighborhood Protection Overlay delays, heating and generator steam hazards at Four Points Apartments, and opposition to the RDU Airport Authority's proposed quarry and 8.3-mile barbed-wire fence near Umstead State Park. Staff presented a $3.861 million LaChase Construction design-build amendment for City Hall HVAC and electrical renovations, updated Council on Willard Street Apartments Phase 1 and Phase 2 LIHTC applications alongside DHA's Liberty Street filings, and unveiled an updated unpaved-roads GIS prioritization study contrasting $12.2 million for asphalt surface treatment against $70+ million for full curb-and-gutter construction over 10 years. In a split appointment vote for the Human Relations Commission Black/African-American male seat, the Clerk reported a 3-3 council tie between Darius Whitney and Terrick Willis (with Mayor Steve Schewel having initially selected Marcus Williams), and Mayor Steve Schewel cast the deciding tie-break vote for Darius Whitney (4-3 for Whitney; individual council ballots in the 3-3 tie were not read into the transcript), before Council unanimously settled the regular agenda 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call and Ceremonial Recognition: Technology Solutions Charity Golf Tournament
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the work session to order at 1:00 p.m. with all seven seated members present. Budget Director Bertha Johnson and Technology Solutions representative John Stinson recognized city employees—including Andrew Holland and Audit Director Jermaine Burlington—for raising over $3,000 for the Boys and Girls Club through the Technology Solutions golf tournament and charity walk.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items, Consent Agenda Review, and Citizens' Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield flagged Item 13/14 (LaChase Construction design-build amendment for City Hall HVAC/electrical renovations) for presentation alongside Consent Items covering HOPWA, Housing for New Hope rapid rehousing and street outreach, police HQ elevator maintenance, DHA security cameras and lighting (Item 12), ST-303 pavement preservation (Item 14), and Public Hearing Item 17 (UDO outdoor lighting). During Citizens' Matters, Ms. Place requested guidance on advancing a Forest Hills Neighborhood Protection Overlay, Lily Lyons reported loud booming noises and dense steam from heating/generator equipment at Four Points Apartments, and a speaker urged Council to file an amicus brief and oppose RDU Airport Authority's Odd Fellows Tract quarry and 8.3-mile barbed-wire fence (with Council agreeing to contact appointee Chuck Hutchinson while deferring lead action to Wake County).

agenda_items.title: Item 13: City Hall HVAC and Electrical Renovations Design-Build Amendment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services staff presented a $3,861,000 construction-phase design-build amendment with LaChase Construction Services LLC within a $5.2 million total project budget for City Hall HVAC and electrical upgrades. Built in 1978 with prior 2009/2011 updates, the building will receive replacement HVAC equipment, ductwork, hot-water piping, lighting updates, and digital controls beginning June 16, including work affecting the second floor and the Mayor and City Council suite.

agenda_items.title: Item 15: Willard Street Apartments Phase 1 & 2 and 2020 LIHTC Applications
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff reported that Willard Street Apartments Phase 1 remained on schedule for certificate of occupancy by year-end with parking deck erection starting soon. For the 2020 9% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) round, Durham partners planned three submissions—Willard Street Phase 2 (Ashton Place seniors housing, because NCHFA prohibits sharing family playground amenities across adjacent phases) and two DHA Liberty Street applications (one family, one senior)—hoping to win at least one (and optimistically two) awards alongside two 4% applications led by Laurel Street.

agenda_items.title: Item 16: Unpaved Roads Study Update and Prioritization Dashboard
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Consultants updated the 2010 Kimley-Horn unpaved roads study, demonstrating a GIS/Esri ArcMap dashboard allowing staff to adjust prioritization weights such as population and maintenance condition. Comparing 10-year life-cycle options ahead of a CIP budget request, presenters contrasted roughly $12.2 million for basic asphalt surface treatment (AST) or plant-mix paving within existing widths against $70+ million for full urban street construction with curb, gutter, sidewalks, utility relocation, and additional right-of-way.

agenda_items.title: Human Relations Commission Appointment Tie-Break and Settling the Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported that Council nominated Aaron Carson for the Human Relations Commission Black/African-American female seat, while the Black/African-American male seat resulted in a 3-3 council tie between Darius Whitney and Terrick Willis (with Mayor Steve Schewel having initially selected Marcus Williams). Mayor Schewel cast the tie-breaking vote for Darius Whitney (his second choice). Council then voted 7-0 by voice to settle the upcoming regular meeting agenda (Consent Items 1–14 and GBA Public Hearing Item 17) and adjourned at 2:28 p.m.
agenda_items.vote_summary: 4-3 Tie-Break for Darius Whitney; 7-0 (Voice) to Settle Agenda
